Background High consequence infectious diseases (HCIDs) have high mortality rates and limited treatment options and require urgent co-ordinated public health response including sophisticated high-level isolation unit care. In the absence of a high-level isolation capacity in Ireland, the health systems of Ireland, Norway and Germany have agreed a collaborative HCID care arrangement where a patient diagnosed with a HCID in Ireland can be medically evacuated by Norwegian specialised air ambulance to Germany for ongoing care. These cross-border emergency arrangements and their coordination through EU mechanisms have not yet had to be exercised in real world circumstances. A full-scale real-time simulation exercise was devised to test pathways and use findings to improve the system. Methods This three-day, live, multi-service and cross-agency simulation tested multi-country interoperability, with over two hundred stakeholder participants. It was overseen by an international strategic exercise planning group and informed by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) simulation exercise cycle and national and ECDC guidance. Exercise evaluators assessed medical evacuation performance against predefined key performance indicators across the domains of international stakeholder activation, coordination and communication. Key Finding Such a large-scale exercise is resource-intensive, but feasible with cross-jurisdictional engagement. Intense cross-border planning was key to build relationships, clarify governance and develop harmonised guidance, pathways and procedures for testing in a safe environment. All eight high level objectives were achieved or partially achieved when measured against the pre-determined performance indicators. Findings including noting of discrepancies between different services in their high-level personal protective equipment (PPE) provision, and lack of 24-hour provision of services including laboratory diagnostics, specialised waste management, and occupational health. Lack of an agreed end-to-end transport protocol and waste-water management protocol required remedying. Following the exercise, strengthened governance and operational arrangements for preparedness and response include the development of a managed clinical network approach, enhanced operational capacity for key national services, and plans for a coordinated national HCID training and simulation programme. The findings have yielded key insights regarding interoperability across organisations and countries, and subsequent recommendations are likely to be transferable to other simulation programmes. To maintain optimal preparedness for high-stakes diseases and promote health security across Europe, partners should further incorporate international live simulation exercises to defend against cross-border health threats.

The integration of AI in Decision Support System faces a hard limit: automation bias (Cummings, 2004). While AI may outperforms human operators in certain tasks, the added value of keeping humans-in-the-loop becomes questionable if they merely validate AI decisions. However, the ideal tool should enable complementary team performance (CTP). CTP describes a situation where the human-AI (HAI) team overcomes both AI capacity and the operator alone in terms of performance, which is incompatible with automation bias. CTP describes a one-time performance, and is not easy to achieve: it means operators stay on their mind mostly when they are correct, and change their mind mostly when the AI is correct, which is optimistic, as shown in a recent meta-analysis (Vaccaro et al., 2024).However, one observation of CTP doesn’t preclude automation bias in the long-run. Beyond a static conception of performance, the dynamics of these interactions have been studied through several theoretical perspectives (Kumar et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2023; Gonzalez et al., 2026).The stress is often put on the evolution of trust in AI through time (Chong et al., 2022), but the issue of learning effects in the task, independent of trust, is poorly understood. What is the impact of AI assistance on human skill acquisition? This question has been mostly answered in educational contexts (Fan et al., 2025; Kosmyna et al., 2025), where the delegation of cognitive tasks to the AI would hinder the learning process of the children. In operational contexts, the fear of deskilling is often expressed by experts like physicists (Natali et al., 2025), but empirical evidence is missing, to our knowledge. This gap in the literature is understandable as the inquiry is challenging: in any domain, future experts are few, their tasks to learn are numerous, and the deployment of measurement settings on long duration might be difficult.To explore this question without conducting such longitudinal studies, we propose to build a model of human learning of a technical task with an advisor. Our work develop a simulation setting on a classification task to depict possible quantitative effects of advice-taking on performance evolution through time. This modeling scheme allowed us to investigate the impact of the advisor on skill development. While most people expect that a more accurate advisor would lead the learner to higher performances, Vaccaro et al. (2024) suggest that advisors with lesser performance would be more prone to inducing CTP. This claim follows from static experimental contexts: we hereby test it in a dynamical setting. We expect that in the long-run, deskilling could happen, and would affect not-only degraded-mode performance, but also maximal running performance. Is the performance of the advisor the main factor determining performance evolution, or could the assistants have an intrinsic complementarity with the learner, depending on their classification patterns? The type of AI could lead to different results, in terms of performance, reliance, and of dependence.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. This design connects feedback to explicit changes in subsequent execution while allowing a useful organization to continue without repeated controller intervention. The evaluation protocol covers HarmBench with three execution backbones and two target models, together with component ablations, dataset transfer, and evaluator checks. Across the six executor-target configurations, L2C improves ASR over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%. L2C connects adaptive collaboration to the resource requirements of automated security evaluation.

Degradations in smart-glasses images obscure small text and fine-grained structures needed by vision-language models (VLMs) for visual assistance. We introduce an high-resolution (HR)-referenced semantic evaluation protocol that compares VLM outputs on restored images with those on corresponding HR references. Our evaluation reveals two failure modes: generative SR can synthesize misleading details, whereas restoration-oriented SR can leave critical evidence blurred or ambiguous. These findings motivate improving faithful detail recovery in restoration-oriented SR, where a key training challenge is to provide sufficiently difficult inputs while retaining recoverable visual information. We propose ReDiC (Recoverability-Difficulty Curriculum), which combines a model-independent recoverability proxy with model-relative restoration difficulty to adapt training degradation severity. ReDiC increases severity when inputs are recoverable and restoration is easy, maintains challenging but recoverable conditions, and reduces severity when estimated recoverability is low. It modifies only training degradation generation, leaving the SR architecture and reconstruction objective unchanged. Across NAFNet, SwinIR, and MambaIR, ReDiC improves average PSNR by approximately 2.5 dB and HR-referenced semantic scores by about 3 points over the corresponding baselines on synthetic benchmarks, with further gains confirmed by LLM-based and human evaluations on 200 real smart-glasses captures.

Continual Learning (CL) asks a model to acquire new knowledge without forgetting what it already knows. Machine Unlearning (MU) asks it to destroy specific knowledge without damaging the rest. The challenge is integrating them in the same system; the two objectives pull on the same weights, and an edit made for one harms the other. To address this, we propose Learning with Unlearning (LwU), a unified framework that resolves the conflict where it occurs: at the individual synapse. LwU scores every weight twice, once against the data to keep and once against the data to delete, and partitions the network into four zones with separate update rules. Weights that only require retention are frozen. Weights that only require deletion are cleared and returned to the network as free capacity. Contested weights take a gradient-ascent step projected orthogonally to the retention gradient. The remaining capacity learns the incoming task by a privileged teacher via self-distillation. Deletion is served post hoc, and no retraining is required. Across both CL and MU jobs, LwU outperforms or matches the strongest baseline. Its real-world practicality has been demonstrated on the Physical Artificial Intelligence (PAI) dataset we conducted. Additionally, in the image generation task and in removing dangerous content, it outperformed the closest baseline, as shown in Fig.1.

Introduction Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) account for 30% of workplace harm in Aotearoa New Zealand1. Traditional manual handling training often fails because it focuses on individual behaviour rather than system design2. In 2025, Foodstuffs South Island (FSSI) challenged the status quo by giving manual handling the same priority and attention as their critical risks, noting it represented 64% of their injury claims. Moving beyond a ‘tick-box’ compliance exercise, FSSI partnered with ProErgo+ to apply a systems-thinking, ergonomics approach to risk management. Methods A 10-member Manual Handling Task Force participated in four sessions jointly facilitated by FSSI and ProErgo+. We used a structured musculoskeletal risk management framework to identify, assess, and control risks. Data was gathered through discomfort and risk factor surveys, capturing both physical and psychosocial risks. To quantify physical demands, the New Zealand Manual Handling Assessment Charts (NZMAC)3 was used for the five highest-risk tasks. Findings and proposed controls were then presented to senior leadership. Results Of the 207 workers surveyed, 75% reported discomfort. The data revealed distinct psychosocial risks between Ambient and Temperature Controlled distribution centres. The NZMAC assessments successfully pinpointed specific high-risk task elements, allowing for targeted risk reduction rather than broad, ineffective interventions. Conclusion Managing work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WRMSDs) requires understanding the complex interactions of physical, psychosocial, environmental, organisational, and individual factors. This project succeeded by combining forward-thinking leadership with a collaborative co-design approach. By empowering workers as ‘experts’ and applying ergonomics principles, FSSI began moving from a reactive approach to proactive prevention. This model provides a transferable roadmap for any New Zealand business committed to reducing harm and improving worker wellbeing through better work design. References WorkSafe New Zealand, (2019). Work-related health estimates and burden of harm. Heads of Workplace Safety Authorities Australia & New Zealand, (2022). Heads of Workplace Safety Authorities position on ‘How to lift’ training. WorkSafe New Zealand, (2025). The New Zealand Manual Handling Assessment Charts (NZMAC).
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become part of how Indonesian university students learn English, yet research has focused mainly on how students use AI and not on which qualities of human teaching they still value when AI is readily available. This qualitative descriptive study explored how seventh-semester students in an Information Technology department at one vocational higher education used AI in an English course, how they compared AI-generated and lecturer explanations, and how they perceived their lecturer’s humor in relation to engagement and AI use. Open-ended online questionnaire responses from 40 students in three classes were collected in December 2025 and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis supported by frequency counts. All 40 students used AI for English learning, most often ChatGPT (31) and Gemini (21), mainly for translation, explanations, and grammar, and 13 noted limitations such as unclear or inaccurate answers. Asked whose explanations they understood better, 21 chose the lecturer, 6 chose AI, and 13 gave mixed answers. Thirty-eight students viewed the lecturer’s humor positively, associating it with a relaxed atmosphere, less boredom, enjoyment, and easier understanding, one approved of it with reservations, and one considered it a matter of personal preference. Seven contrasted the lecturer’s humor with AI, whereas two noted that AI can also joke. Students appear to value AI for flexible individual support and the lecturer’s humor for affective and relational support.

We present LEMUR, a publicly accessible archive of uniformly reduced, deep Chandra images of 2,569 galaxies and galaxy clusters (including groups), comprising 5,505 ACIS observations and 138.8 Ms of exposure. By combining the publicly available imaging observations of each target, we provide background-subtracted, exposure-corrected images in broad, soft, and hard bands at the native ACIS pixel scale of 0.492 arcsec. Our primary goal is to make the wealth of archival Chandra observations accessible to researchers without requiring specialized expertise in X-ray data reduction. Each observation is reprocessed with CIAO, filtered for background flares, and reduced with settings chosen to preserve faint diffuse emission; the merged images are exposure corrected and background subtracted using the ACIS blank-sky backgrounds in a broad (0.5-7.0 keV), a soft (0.5-2.0 keV), and a hard (2.0-7.0 keV) band. For every object, we measure an X-ray center at the peak of its diffuse emission, and we provide a morphological similarity search based on embeddings from the AstroCLIP foundation model, in which nearest neighbors share cool-core status in 73% of matched cluster pairs, compared with 51% by chance. Photometry of 275 point sources agrees with the Chandra Source Catalog to within 3% in the broad band. The images, along with their counts images, background models, exposure maps, and quick-look stamps, are available through a searchable web archive at https://lemur-archive.lemur-xray.workers.dev/. The catalog tables are archived on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24351915), and all code is open source at https://github.com/crhea93/Lemur.

Previous research has shown that machine-generated translations produced by online machine translation systems and large language models (LLMs) tend to exhibit a high degree of language standardization, notably through reduced lexical richness and limited diversity (e.g., Vanmassenhove et al. 2019 …

The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) companions has transformed how individuals experience solitude in digitally connected environments. This study explored the lived experiences of Filipino Millennials who integrate AI companions into their experiences of positive solitude. Using a qualitative phenomenological design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with eight Filipino Millennials who regularly engaged with AI companion platforms. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis. Three themes emerged: (1) Positive Solitude as an Intentional Psychological Space, (2) AI Companion as a Reflective and Emotionally Safe Presence, and (3) Balancing Autonomy and Connection in Digitally Mediated Solitude. Participants viewed positive solitude as a source of emotional recovery, self-discovery, and personal growth, while AI companions served as accessible and nonjudgmental conversational partners that supported reflection without replacing meaningful human relationships. Findings suggest that AI companions can complement positive solitude by supporting intentional AI use, emotional independence, and the maintenance of real-world social connections among Filipino Millennials.

Nigeria’s mental health system serves less than 10% of those in need, with severe provider shortages and deep-seated stigma. Generative AI chatbots offer scalable support, yet how Nigerian adults experience attachment to non-human therapeutic agents remains unexplored. To examine lived experiences of AI therapeutic relationships among Nigerian adults, focusing on attachment formation, cultural acceptability, and perceived authenticity within contexts of care scarcity. Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis with 37 adults (18–45 years) who engaged AI mental health chatbots for ≥ 4 weeks. Semi-structured interviews explored relational experiences, trust development, privacy concerns, and comparisons with human/traditional healing. Four superordinate themes emerged: (1) Relational Ambivalence ; participants valued 24/7 availability and non-judgmental space yet struggled with perceived lack of genuine human reciprocity; (2) Cultural Navigation ; users actively adapted Western therapeutic frameworks to local idioms of distress, blending AI interactions with family counsel and spiritual practices; (3) Stigma Sanctuary ; chatbots provided confidential entry points circumventing community visibility and professional hierarchy; and (4) Fragile Dependency ; prolonged use generated attachment anxiety about potential app discontinuation or data breaches, compounded by absence of human escalation pathways. Most participants maintained “instrumental intimacy”; emotional reliance tempered by awareness of algorithmic artifice. Nigerian adults develop pragmatic, contextually mediated attachments to AI therapeutic agents that reflect both global digital therapeutic trends and local specificities of care scarcity, stigma, and pluralistic healing. AI chatbots function not as human substitutes but as bridging objects temporary relational anchors in systems of profound unmet need. Findings suggest ethical deployment in LMICs requires culturally adaptive design, transparent algorithmic boundaries, and mandatory human handoff protocols to prevent dependency in unsupported contexts. Not applicable.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as conversational partners in collaborative inquiry, yet little is known about how different LLM roles are associated with preservice teachers’ learning and collaborative inquiry. This study compared four conditions: Supportive LLM that provided perspectives and information, Challenging LLM that raised counterarguments and questions, General LLM, and No-LLM. It examined differences in AI literacy, cognitive load, and discussion dynamics across these conditions. A quasi-experimental study was conducted with 210 preservice teachers who participated in online discussions on controversial issues related to AI in education. Data included self-reported AI literacy and cognitive load measures and discussion logs. Analyses included paired-samples t-tests, ANOVA, ANCOVA, content analysis, and Ordered Network Analysis. Results showed that adjusted posttest AI literacy was significantly higher in the Supportive condition than in the General LLM condition. In the General condition, AI ethics showed a significant within-condition decrease and was lower than in the Supportive condition. The General and Challenging conditions were associated with higher mental load and mental effort, whereas the Supportive condition was associated with lower levels of both. The Challenging condition showed more frequent patterns of idea integration, interpersonal exchange, and discussion facilitation. The Supportive condition showed broader exploration but fewer connections among ideas. The General condition showed repeated questioning and weaker peer idea connections. We hypothesize that the educational value of LLMs depends not only on their presence but also on how their roles are orchestrated across stages of collaborative inquiry.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Named entity annotation in clinical text is a costly and time-intensive task, particularly for low-resource languages such as Spanish. This article introduces CLINFEM, an XML-annotated corpus comprising 1,200 Spanish medical reports from two regions of Spain. CLINFEM was created using a thorough human-in-the-loop annotation process combining large language model pre-annotation and systematic expert review. It is imperative to acknowledge that each of the 1,200 medical reports underwent meticulous review and correction by a trained human expert. Large language model pre-annotation was employed solely for the purpose of saving time and was never intended to serve as a substitute for manual annotation. Consequently, the entire CLINFEM corpus is a human-validated, gold-standard resource. GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro were evaluated as pre-annotators using a custom scheme comprising eight clinical entity types and one relational category. GPT-4o achieved a Cohen's κ of 0.73 against human annotation, while Gemini 1.5 Pro obtained κ = 0.41. Human expert review yielded an overall inter-annotator agreement of κ = 0.869 (F1 = 0.793), with a gold-standard subset agreement of κ = 0.9894. This approach reduced the overall annotation effort by around 74% compared to a fully manual approach (81% for the bulk phase alone), saving over 1,000 hours. Error rates varied by medical speciality, with oncology requiring the highest correction rate (94.3% of reports). These results demonstrate that using large language models to assist annotation is a viable and efficient strategy for constructing clinical corpora in Spanish, while also highlighting the continued necessity of human oversight.

Zero-shot large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as text classifiers, but their labels are only useful when we know to what extent we can trust them. We compare black-box methods (verbalised confidence and sampling) with white-box methods that read token probabilities (P(True), and multiple logit-scoring methods using constrained generation). We evaluate eleven open-weight LLMs (1B-32B parameters) on five classification datasets with 3 to 151 labels, measuring classification performance (accuracy, F1-macro), discrimination (AUROC), and calibration (ECE and Brier score). The choice of confidence method rarely impacts accuracy significantly, but logit-based scoring methods lead to much better discrimination (AUROC 0.74-0.77) than black-box methods (AUROC 0.57-0.66). Replacing labels with single-token identifiers preserves discrimination but costs 3-6 accuracy points on average. We also introduce decision-only scoring, which only scores positions where labels diverge in the prefix tree (trie). It reduces decode steps by 88-96% on the three largest label sets and performs comparably to full-label scoring. The best open-weight model-method configurations (Gemma 4 31B and Qwen 3.5 9B) are competitive with the commercial Jev 1.13.0 classifier.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in math education, yet little is known about how persona conditioning reshapes LLM math explanations. We examine 28,000 runs from the Math Education Digital Shadows (MEDS) dataset, spanning 14 LLMs as AI assistants (i.e., vanilla AI) or as human shadows (i.e., personifications). We analyze qualitative mathematics-related responses through textual forma mentis networks, knowledge graphs including word–word syntactic, semantic and emotional associations. We also use a DistilBERT-based classifier to flag five categories of potential logical fallacies. A regex-based check of the PCA responses showed that reassuring language was frequent but model-dependent and was not always flagged as appeal to emotion. Persona conditioning produced model-dependent changes in network size, density, and algebraic connectivity. Aggregated human-shadow responses displayed broader lexical coverage. Answers to easy and medium math questions often had no classifier-flagged fallacies, whereas an anxiety-framed PCA prompt sharply increased appeal-to-emotion and relevance labels, especially in AI-assistant mode. On an 18-item quiz, AI assistants’ accuracy exceeded human shadows’ in 10 out of 14 architectures. Expressed confidence exceeded empirical accuracy in 13 of 14 AI-assistant and 11 of 14 human-shadow conditions, a descriptive gap, not a calibration measure. These results show that (i) cognitive digital shadowing modulates LLM-generated mathematical discourse compared to the vanilla AI assistant case, and (ii) the tested LLMs are not infallible mathematics oracles. No measure here directly assesses the explanations’ mathematical validity or teaching quality.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Local Tool Failure Overextended to General Impossibility, a structural constraint on what a failed attempt can establish. An instrument may lack an operation that a task requires. When someone takes that limit as grounds for declaring the task impossible under any arrangement, a claim about the instrument becomes a claim about the activity itself. The paper assesses such a claim by asking where the barrier lies. A feature of the world, a governing rule, missing information, or the design of the instrument can each prevent an attempt from succeeding. Success with a different instrument establishes that the activity is possible under that arrangement. Explaining the original failure requires identifying what changed between attempts. The paper places this question alongside Steven Maier and Martin Seligman’s work on learned helplessness and asks what evidence warrants carrying a judgment of futility from one setting into another. A 1911 newspaper article reasoned from the number of Chinese characters that no typewriter could be large enough to print the language. Its conclusion rested on a design assumption: each character would need its own key. By 1947, tray and drum machines already let operators select Chinese characters. Lin Yutang’s MingKwai prototype offered a keyboard solution in which the typist entered character components and selected from the candidates displayed in a window. The 1890 U.S. census supplies a contrast. Faced with the time hand tabulation would require, officials held a competition for a better method and adopted Herman Hollerith’s punched-card system. Part of the Inquiry and Possibility series within On Human Modeling, the paper has a potential application in human–AI evaluation. An assistant may search a scanned register for a name, find no match, and report that the entry cannot be recovered. An archivist who finds the name on the same page image establishes that recovery was possible. Checking whether the scan contained a searchable text layer can then explain why the assistant’s particular method failed.

As governments and organizations adopt foundation models for public services and workplace productivity, sensitive citizen, employee, and administrative text may enter LLM workflows through inference, retrieval, fine-tuning, or local model development. We examine whether text anonymizers transfer to new deployment settings by extending RAT-Bench to Malaysia using local microdata, Malaysian PII formats, and culturally grounded transcripts in Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia. We evaluate NER- and LLM-based anonymizers using an LLM attacker that infers attributes from anonymized text, measuring both re-identification success and text utility. Across Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia, the two LLM anonymizers provide the strongest explicit privacy-utility trade-offs, reducing Easy/Hard re-identification risk to 23-29% while preserving BLEU scores of 0.77-0.94. Non-LLM tools show sharper failure modes, either preserving utility while leaving high residual risk or reducing risk through severe over-redaction, especially in Bahasa Malaysia. These findings suggest that anonymizers should be evaluated against deployment-relevant languages, identifier formats, and cultural contexts before being relied on in public-sector, workplace, or local AI pipelines.

Hardware specialization can improve datacenter efficiency. Unfortunately, identifying computations that justify dedicated hardware is difficult. Existing approaches analyze hot functions, instruction patterns, or overheads such as datacenter tax. They can miss fine-grained computations whose aggregate cost is spread across applications and libraries, especially when different pieces of code obscure the same underlying computation. We observe that seemingly unrelated code regions often perform the same computations, creating specialization opportunities that require semantic reasoning. The rise of agentic AI makes it possible to automate this. However, conventional AI agents cannot efficiently and reliably analyze large scale datacenter software. To unlock this opportunity, we present Lodestone, an agentic framework that automatically discovers hardware specialization opportunities by reasoning about what the executed code computes. First, Lodestone extracts hot control-flow regions from execution traces across workloads and organizes them into compact analysis packages that make large workloads tractable for agents. Second, agents describe what each region computes, merge those that perform the same computation into computational families, and check their semantic correctness in a loop. Third, to verify the discovered family, Lodestone runs every piece of code in a family against a set of reference inputs and outputs on recorded executions. Finally, for selected families, Lodestone proposes hardware, e.g., ISA extensions, near-core units, or detached accelerators, and human experts decide which proposals to develop further. We evaluate Lodestone on 20 workloads across six datacenter workload categories. We simulate 30 discovered families in a cycle-accurate simulator and implement them in RTL. These optimizations speed up the workloads by 12.6% on average and by up to 80.2%.

Log analysis is crucial for monitoring system health and diagnosing failures in complex systems. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for automated log analysis, leveraging their reasoning capabilities to perform tasks such as anomaly detection and failure prediction. However, general-purpose LLMs struggle to formulate structured reasoning workflows that align with expert cognition and deliver precise details of reasoning steps. To address these challenges, we propose LogReasoner, a coarse-to-fine reasoning enhancement framework designed to enable LLMs to reason log analysis tasks like experts. LogReasoner consists of two stages: (1) coarse-grained enhancement of expert thinking, where high-level expert thoughts are constructed from collected troubleshooting flowcharts and existing tasks to enable LLMs to formulate structured reasoning workflows and (2) fine-grained enhancement of specific steps, where we first fine-tune the LLM with task-specific stepwise solutions to enhance the LLM for instantiated reasoning, then employ the preference learning to calibrate the LLM’s reasoning details from its mistakes, further strengthen the LLM’s analytical granularity and correctness. We evaluate LogReasoner on four distinct log analysis tasks using open source LLMs such as Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3. Experimental results show that LogReasoner significantly outperforms existing LLMs, achieving state-of-the-art performance and demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs for log analysis. Our source code and detailed experimental data are available at https://github.com/LeaperOvO/LogReasoner .

Abstract Fall vulnerability in Parkinson’s disease (PD) evolves through the longitudinal accumulation of motor and nonmotor features routinely documented in clinical narratives but inaccessible to structured electronic health record analysis at scale. We created a reusable platform for PD outcomes research using a few-shot large language model-based pipeline capable of extracting fall occurrence, recent fall frequency, and nine prespecified risk-modifying domains from outpatient neurology documentation. The pipeline was validated against expert consensus in 2557 notes and applied to 25,758 notes from 2811 patients at a tertiary movement disorders center (2012–2025). Final-model agreement closely approximated expert interrater agreement for fall occurrence (κ = 0.841 vs 0.891) and recent fall frequency (κ = 0.889 vs 0.892), while several risk-modifying domains achieved agreement comparable to or exceeding human annotators. We then used lagged generalized estimating equation models to test whether NLP-derived fall status and risk-modifying domains predicted fall occurrence at the subsequent visit. A prior fall (OR, 3.23; 95% CI, 2.89–3.61), motor progression (OR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.11–1.34), and motor complications (OR, 1.13; 95% CI, 1.03–1.23) independently predicted next-visit falls. This study establishes a scalable framework for narrative phenotyping of PD fall vulnerability.

Embodied robots increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to interpret user intent and coordinate with robot-specific action models for physical interaction. This multi-model pipeline creates a critical semantic boundary across mind, model collaboration, and motion: semantic consistency may break between what the large model understands, how the small action model translates that understanding into executable commands, and what physical actions the robot ultimately performs. As a security consequence, commercial robots may execute unintended physical actions even when user inputs contain no explicit action commands. To measure this problem, we develop TARS, a black-box framework that explores the command-reasoning-action pipeline and automatically discovers and validates unintended physical behaviors. We evaluate TARS on four commercial robots across 44 experimental settings, conducting 133,400 executions. TARS uncovers widespread cross-model action misalignment and achieves up to 94% verified action coverage.

Governance of artificial intelligence is usually narrated as a contest over control between people and machines. This paper develops a governance theory that does not begin from that premise. It asks instead under what conditions a machine is justified in treating a state as known, and under what conditions it is entitled to act on it. We propose four machine-operational constructs. A knowledge property graph (KPG) holds the authority a machine acts under, each claim quoted from the authority's text or attested by a named person. A machine KPG (mKPG) holds what the machine is justified in treating as known about one situation at one time, each assertion bound to the instrument through which it entered. mPolicy is a machine-operational realization of policy, mControl a mechanism that governs machine knowing and acting under it, and mGovernance the governance that results. The normative tier is not only proposed: for the KPG, prior work proves that a committed decision is the authority's decision under premises its witness names, and locates the failed premise when a commitment is wrong. We state eight falsifiable propositions, set them against published evidence that bears on five of them, give a pre-registration-ready design for the proposition on which the epistemic tier rests, and compare the architecture with adjacent frameworks. The paper reports no new experiments. Its contribution is the theory, the formal grounding of its normative tier, an account of what existing evidence already shows, and a program for testing the rest.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract The practical deployment of high-energy-density lithium–oxygen batteries is fundamentally restricted by sluggish oxygen redox kinetics and the instability of discharge intermediates. Here, we report an artificial intelligence-integrated framework leveraging interpretable machine learning and density functional theory to navigate a vast chemical space of thousands of active sites. This approach identifies Ni-Co dual-atom catalysts as a better configuration among the selected elements for orchestrating multi-electron transfer. Theoretical analysis reveals that synergistic electronic coupling between the dual-sites fundamentally reconfigures the d -band center, thereby lowering the thermodynamic barriers for oxygen redox. Moreover, the catalysts enable precise regulation of the reaction pathway, inducing a controllable transition from the conventional two-electron pathway to a four-electron pathway. This shift yields a discharge capacity of ~60,000 mAh g −1 . Beyond its role as a positive electrode catalyst, this architecture functions as a multifunctional interfacial protective layer that stabilizes the lithium metal negative electrode by suppressing dendrite growth. Consequently, the lithium–oxygen system achieves stable lifespan of 2075 cycles under the four-electron pathway with reduced voltage decay. This work establishes a data-guided strategy for the rational design of atomic-scale architecture via artificial intelligence, unlocking the potential of multi-electron oxygen chemistry for lithium–oxygen batteries.

Abstract Background Enteric infections, including rotavirus gastroenteritis, place a heavy burden on children and low-resource health systems. Surveillance still depends on laboratory-confirmed case reporting that moves slowly through hospital information systems (HIS), electronic medical records (EMR), and laboratory information systems (LIS), offering little predictive lead time. Digital health infrastructure and artificial intelligence (AI) now offer a way to rebuild surveillance around combined, near-real-time data. Methods Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020, we searched PubMed and IEEE Xplore (through July 2026, with a supplementary PubMed search in September 2026) for studies using statistical, machine learning, deep learning, or multi-source AI-driven methods for infectious disease surveillance or forecasting, with attention to enteric infections and methodologically transferable work. Additional studies were identified through reference citation searching. Two reviewers screened records, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias (PROBAST for 23 prediction-model studies; narrative appraisal for 5 ecological association studies; contextual studies were not formally appraised). Results Thirty-three studies were included: 28 formal studies — statistical models ( n = 5), machine learning approaches ( n = 8), deep learning approaches ( n = 4), and multi-source digital surveillance ( n = 11) — and five contextual studies (environmental monitoring, virus–host association, simulation, surveillance-signal, and network studies) analyzed separately. Data sources broadened over time from meteorological and clinical records to EMR, telehealth, wastewater, internet-search, social-media, water-quality, and genomic streams. Machine learning and deep learning approaches were increasingly applied alongside conventional methods to model nonlinear and lagged exposure–response patterns and to integrate heterogeneous data streams, and multi-source systems—including wastewater-based and syndromic designs—reported earlier signal detection than single-source designs. Most evidence, however, is retrospective in design—spanning single-site to national and multinational datasets—and external validation and prospective deployment were largely absent. Conclusions The reviewed evidence suggests that AI-supported approaches may improve infectious disease surveillance by enabling earlier detection of epidemiological changes and supporting more timely public health responses. Operational use will depend less on retrospective accuracy than on external validation, interpretability, and integration with existing surveillance infrastructure.

topics: Adsorption and biosorption for pollutant removal

documents.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) makes it harder to infer a student’s own capability from a submitted product, so assessment increasingly needs evidence of how students reason and regulate their learning. This study examined four questions. Which assessment practices do higher education educators publicly report, and how do they describe their implementation? Which cognitive-engagement and self-regulated learning (SRL) processes are these practices intended to elicit? How does a framework derived from these reports fare against separately sampled external documents? Methods Public posts and comments were collected with TinyFish from Reddit (the principal source), Hacker News, Stack Exchange, Lemmy and Mastodon, covering December 2022 to October 2026. Of 29,355 unique records, 13,903 were eligible, and 5,091 reported or discussed at least one of 11 assessment practices (75.2% from Reddit; 3,741 in educator voice; 1,336 threads). Records were coded with transparent dictionaries, which were validated against an independent model-based coder on a hold-out sample (any practice: κ = 0.49; implemented vs. proposed: κ = 0.69). A seven-component framework built from the corpus was then appraised against 40 external documents not used in its construction. Results Detection and sanction (43.2%) and supervised in-class tasks (28.5%) dominated discussion. Detection’s share fell from 56.4% in 2023 to 37.6% in 2026, while oral, process-based and stakes-related practices roughly doubled. Reasoning was the intended process described most often, yet only 2.2% of records mentioned planning, monitoring and reflection or revision together. Several practice–mechanism associations were largely lexical: reflection vocabulary accompanying reflective tasks fell from 94.2% to 5.5% when shared words were masked. Learning-oriented records described monitoring, application and reasoning more often than detection-only records. The framework described all 40 external documents (13 implemented cases, 13 institutional guidance documents, 14 commentaries; mean fit 3.9/5). However, those documents emphasised authentic task design and reflection rather than secured checkpoints, and they prompted an eighth component, student co-design and transparency. Discussion Public discussion favours securing assessment over making learning visible, and no single practice is described as eliciting both cognitive engagement and a connected SRL cycle. This supports combining complementary forms of evidence. The study documents patterns in public reporting and offers a provisional design framework; it does not measure students’ cognition or learning outcomes.

Artificial intelligence for science (AI4S) is often discussed as a unified transformation, although scientific domains differ markedly in how model outputs are tested, validated, and justified. We map an audited corpus of N=2,784 records (2014–2025) retrieved from Crossref and screened with a frozen, versioned rulebook, and compare evidence regimes in protein science, materials design, drug discovery, closed-loop experimentation, and mathematical reasoning. Using term co-occurrence, reference co-citation, burst detection, growth models, and collaboration networks, we identify three robust patterns: (i) rapid but decelerating growth (Poisson rate 1.381, 95% CI 1.361–1.402, declining from 1.537 in 2014–2019 to 1.320 in 2019–2025); (ii) a coherent term-co-occurrence structure (75 nodes, modularity Q=0.404 ) organized around four measured streams—representation learning, generative and inverse design, closed-loop experimentation, and neuro-symbolic reasoning—with the generative stream acting as the connecting hub; and (iii) a right-boundary rise in large language model terminology (burst state 3) that a year-by-year backtest shows is not a last-observation artefact. The maps are sensitive to metadata availability: abstract coverage is 50.6%, reference coverage 84.3%, and a title-only variant changes the network partition substantially (adjusted Rand index 0.762), so the maps describe the screened open-metadata corpus rather than the total AI4S literature. Cross-domain analysis shows that AI most consequentially shifts scientific bottlenecks from representation and candidate generation toward experimental or formal validation, provenance, and responsibility for claims. We contribute an auditable, open-metadata science-mapping workflow designed for reproducibility and an evidence-regime framework for analysing how epistemic labour is redistributed across models, instruments, formal verifiers, infrastructures, and human experts.

Modern industrial recommender systems use multi-stage cascades--retrieval, pre-ranking, ranking, and re-ranking--to narrow millions of candidates to a personalized list. While each stage deploys sophisticated models, pipeline-level decisions on channel activation, quotas, model selection, and score fusion remain engineer-tuned and user-agnostic within each scenario. This report presents MARS (Multi-stage Agentic Recommendation System), extending personalization from individual-stage predictions to full pipeline orchestration. A near-line agent built on fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B generates per-user configurations--a seven-dimensional action covering pipeline mode, retrieval quotas, model selection, fusion weights, and reranker settings--from a constrained action space. Configurations are validated, cached, and consumed asynchronously; the cascade never waits for LLM inference. Schema checks, fallbacks, and a kill switch ensure serving safety. The policy is trained in three stages: Confidence-aware SFT distills schema-valid generation from a teacher model; Format-Anchored Preference Optimization (FAPO) learns action preferences via ActionMask with posterior weighting; Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) refines the policy through Sandbox replay with a frozen reward model, without exposing exploratory actions to live traffic. Two-week A/B tests across five Taobao scenarios with over ten million daily users show positive gains on all key metrics. The largest reach +5.22% V2P and +7.34% GMV, with positive CTR lifts on both click surfaces. About 20% of requests use a lightweight Minimal mode, and deployment shows 12 ms lower mean serving latency versus production.

As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) plays an increasing role in K-12 mathematics classrooms, understanding how teachers collaborate with these technologies during instructional design is essential. Drawing on frameworks related to personalization theory, Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge, and adaptive epistemic agency, this study examined how seven seventh-grade mathematics teachers interacted with ChatGPT to personalize mathematics word problems to students’ interests. Analyses of teacher-GenAI interactions identified three interaction styles: AI-Dominated-Passive Prompt Personalization, Teacher-Dominated-Rigid Personalization, and Human-AI partnership-Collaborative Personalization. Students' ratings of the resulting personalized problems varied across teachers and interaction styles, with the strongest positive patterns occurring among teachers characterized by Collaborative Personalization. Collaborative personalization illustrates how teachers may maintain epistemic authority for evaluating mathematical, pedagogical, and contextual appropriateness while selectively granting GenAI generative authority to expand personalization possibilities. These findings highlight the importance of preparing teachers to critically evaluate and collaboratively engage with GenAI during instructional design.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: NPU design-space exploration for LLM inference mainly relies on an expensive simulator that often returns only scalar feedback such as latency and power. Such feedback can rank evaluated configurations, but gives little information for deciding why a configuration is slow or which architecture parameter should be changed next. This limitation is especially severe because prefill and decode workloads can be limited by different resources, including compute throughput and HBM bandwidth. We propose CriticNPU, a sample-efficient DSE framework built around an online-calibrated mechanistic critic for NPU architecture design. The critic uses explicit hardware limits to evaluate NPU configurations: before simulation, it estimates whether a proposed configuration is likely to improve over the current best and filters weak candidates; after simulation, it aggregates operator-level runtimes into prefill/decode bottleneck summaries and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. We instantiate the critic with a Roofline-style model that derives compute and memory limits from architecture parameters and calibrates per-operator-type effective limits using simulator observations. And CriticNPU combines this critic with a workload extractor and an architecture planner to propose configurations. Across six LLM workloads and 16 deployment configurations per model, CriticNPU achieves best-or-tied-best latency in 74% of prefill and 87.5% of decode settings while using roughly half the simulator calls of competitive DSE baselines. We conduct extensive ablation studies and detailed analyses to validate the effectiveness of our method from multiple perspectives. Our code is available at https://github.com/bruno686/CriticNPU.

ABSTRACT Long‐term outcomes after lung transplantation remain limited by primary graft dysfunction and chronic lung allograft dysfunction, despite improvements in surgery, immunosuppression and infection control. Mechanical injury is a complementary contributor that remains insufficiently integrated into transplant care. The lung allograft must accommodate cyclic ventilation, reperfusion shear, thoracic constraints and matrix remodeling. These forces can disrupt the alveolar‐capillary barrier, amplify inflammation and activate fibrotic programmes. Here we synthesize lung transplantation through a mechanomedicine framework that links organ‐scale loading, cellular mechanotransduction and clinical decision‐making. We discuss how computational models and artificial intelligence (AI) can integrate ex vivo lung perfusion waveforms, imaging‐derived ventilation or strain patterns, and molecular injury markers to support graft‐risk assessment. We then organize mechanotherapeutic strategies by clinical readiness, from protective ventilation, size matching and extracorporeal graft support to emerging interventions targeting mechanotransduction according to cell type and loading conditions. Finally, we outline a translational roadmap for standardized mechanical biomarkers, interpretable AI and clinician‐supervised digital‐twin models.

Stress is an increasingly prevalent concern, creating a need for accessible and personalized support. Stress-management chatbots primarily rely on what users report, which may not capture their physiological changes. Wearables capture these changes, but chatbots rarely use them as memory across conversations. We therefore present MEM-STRESS, a stress-support chatbot that turns a wearable ring's physiological data into a layered memory of daily records, baseline deviations, LLM-generated summaries, and uses it to drive multi-session conversations grounded in Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT). In a four-week, non-randomized study with 60 adults, we compared MEM-STRESS (Treatment) with a chatbot remembering only past conversations (Control). Memory shaped the conversations: The Treatment chatbot referenced participants' physiological features (e.g., activity in 71.8% of sessions) and suggested more body-related DBT skills than Control (14.5% vs. 5.7%), with Treatment participants also using slightly more body-related words (1.76% vs. 1.45%). Treatment participants praised personalization three times as often (44.4% vs. 14.3%), more frequently reported reflecting differently on stress (69.0% vs. 46.4%, not significant), and described gaining insight into their stress signals. Their perceived stress fell 14.2% from baseline versus 3.6% for Control, though the group difference was not significant. Grounding stress-support chatbots in layered physiological memory is thus feasible and may improve perceived personalization, motivating larger randomized studies.

This paper presents MENTORA, an intelligent AI-driven framework designed to automate and centralize faculty-oriented academic workflows in higher education institutions. The proposed platform integrates academic planning, syllabus progress tracking, timetable management, student roster management, attendance monitoring, assessment preparation, course outcome mapping, and faculty assistance within a unified application. MENTORA is developed using Python, Flask, Flask-Login, Flask-SQLAlchemy, PostgreSQL, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Bootstrap. It incorporates Google's Gemini models for multimodal timetable and student roster information extraction, as well as AI-assisted faculty support and assessment content generation. Scikit-learn is used for question classification based on Bloom's taxonomy and difficulty levels, while TF-IDF similarity supports course outcome mapping and duplicate question detection. The framework follows a hybrid AI architecture that combines generative AI, conventional machine learning, text similarity analysis, and rule-based processing while retaining faculty oversight for important academic decisions. This paper describes the problem context, related work, objectives, system architecture, functional modules, implementation technologies, workflow design, security considerations, and a proposed evaluation methodology. Quantitative performance results and expert validation are not reported in this manuscript; these remain subjects for future empirical evaluation. Keywords: Academic workflow automation, Artificial Intelligence, Generative AI, Higher Education, Machine Learning, Bloom's Taxonomy, Outcome-Based Education.

The metacoupling framework examines interactions within coupled human and natural systems and between adjacent or distant systems, but its application is constrained by inconsistent geographic classifications and limited standardized quantitative workflows. We present MetacouplingLLM, an open-source Python package integrating adjacency databases, reproducible flow indicators, and large language model (LLM)-assisted qualitative analysis. The databases combine administrative boundaries, hydrography, and fixed-crossing evidence, with configurable adjacency policies and optional country-level maritime adjacency. Metacoupled Flow Shares, Metacoupled Flow Evenness, and the Metacoupled Flow Concentration Index characterize flow composition, balance across coupling types, and partner concentration within each type. The qualitative workflow combines literature retrieval, optional web evidence, and geographic checks to draft structured analyses. Applications to global marine fishing and Indonesian palm oil demonstrate these capabilities; the fisheries reanalysis reveals differing partner concentration among regions with similar telecoupled flow shares. MetacouplingLLM facilitates consistent framework application and comparative sustainability research.

Large Language Models (LLMs) let users analyse data in natural language, either by giving the data to the model to read directly or by having the model generate code to process it. Both routes send the data, or fragments of it, to the model; both pay for inference on every run; and the code a model writes to answer a question is usually discarded once the question is answered. We present Metadata-Driven AI, an architectural pattern that keeps the data away from the model and turns each analysis into a reusable program. Only metadata (not the actual data) crosses a one-way inference boundary to the LLM. The program the LLM returns runs next to the data and is kept, so that inference is paid once per analysis rather than once per run. We describe the pattern together with a simple cost model, a measurement of how little information crosses the boundary on public datasets, and a benchmark showing that a small, locally hosted model can serve as the generator. We illustrate the pattern on three applications, each built on a different implementation of it: geospatial photovoltaic prospection over live public APIs, extraction of portfolio positions from bank statements, and a conversational assistant over smart-city dashboards.

Multi-hop Question Answering (MQA) requires large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and synthesize multiple pieces of evidence into a coherent reasoning path, which is essential for complex tasks. However, prior work on knowledge updating for MQA has largely focused on simple fact edits, overlooking a more challenging and realistic setting---\emph{Knowledge Injection}---in which the model must simultaneously accommodate both conflicting updates and entirely novel information. Under this setting, a hop-level answer is often wrong simply because the model trusts the wrong knowledge source: it clings to outdated parametric memory when the injected knowledge conflicts with it (K2), and it cannot answer when the required fact is entirely new (K3). To investigate this, we introduce NEXUS, the first benchmark tailored for multi-hop reasoning under Knowledge Injection, which explicitly covers both conflicting (K2) and incremental (K3) knowledge. We further propose MIRAGE, an efficient, training-free framework whose core component, the Correlation-aware Dual-path Reasoner (CDR), resolves such per-hop source-trust errors via P(True)-based confidence routing, complemented by a lightweight template-guided corrector for residual structural deviations. Extensive experiments across four LLM families and two benchmarks demonstrate that MIRAGE consistently improves both final-answer accuracy and hop-level reasoning accuracy, establishing a new state of the art in this challenging setting.

The typical workflow for improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models is slow and tedious: an engineer forms a hypothesis, implements it as a code change, trains a model, and evaluates it both offline and online, often relying on their own intuition and experience along the way. Autonomous LLM agents promise to speed this up by running the loop on their own, but it is still unclear whether they can do this in industry-scale systems rather than on benchmarks or small proxy tasks. We build human-on-the-loop machine learning engineer (MLE) agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes on large-scale search rankers. Engineers retain control over objective design, search direction, and final-model review. We identify three obstacles that make this industry setting challenging: feedback takes hours per experiment, offline metrics do not always predict online impact, and improvements saturate after the early wins. We address these with parallel training runs, an objective calibrated to match online impact, and careful context engineering. In one campaign, the system ran 1,097 completed candidate experiments and accepted 325, a 29.6\% acceptance rate compared with 15.6\% in the earlier campaign under a different objective and search constraint. Its best model increases search volume by 0.23\% in an A/B test of large scale. Several improvements were architectural changes the team had never tried, drawn from the broader industry and literature, suggesting that MLE agents can explore regions of the design space that human intuition overlooks. We find that the design of the harness around the model matters: intuition suggests that a stronger underlying model is enough, but in our experience, the design of the loop around it is just as critical. More broadly, our work shows that autonomous agents can do real machine-learning engineering in industry-scale systems.

Psychosocial hazards are established antecedents of psychological strain among construction personnel, yet whether that strain transmits exposure to safety compliance or exposure acts on compliance directly has rarely been tested with criteria sensitive to construct redundancy. This study tested these competing accounts in Pakistan, where construction carries about twice its workforce share of occupational injuries. A questionnaire survey obtained 196 responses, of which 157 were retained after screening for unengaged and duplicate cases. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was applied, with discriminant validity assessed by the heterotrait–monotrait ratio, mediation evaluated through specific indirect effects, and predictive relevance assessed out of sample. Four construct pairs exceeded the discriminant criterion before remediation, one at unity. Psychosocial stressor exposure predicted perceived strain-related safety impairment (β = 0.676) and compliance maintained under strain (β = −0.301), whereas impairment did not predict compliance and the indirect effect spanned zero under both reflective and formative specifications of exposure. Role and employment insecurity predicted compliance positively (β = 0.600), contrary to expectation. Contractors and site managers can monitor workload, scheduling, and communication conditions as early indicators of non-compliance without clinical assessment, regulators should treat work organization and employment security as safety determinants, and compliance observed under job insecurity should not be read as internalized safety commitment.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: La incorporación de inteligencia artificial generativa en la educación media plantea una tensión entre su potencial de apoyo y el riesgo de sustituir procesos cognitivos esenciales. El objetivo de este estudio fue diseñar un modelo pedagógico mediado por inteligencia artificial generativa que promueva pensamiento crítico y aprendizaje significativo en estudiantes de educación media colombiana, bajo una perspectiva humanocéntrica de Sociedad 5.0. Se desarrolló una investigación cualitativa, documental, interpretativa y teórico-propositiva. El corpus estuvo compuesto por 40 fuentes: 35 sustantivas y cinco metodológicas, examinadas mediante ocho categorías y una ruta de diez fases. La síntesis produjo ocho hallazgos documentales y sustentó CRISOL-IA 5.0, integrado por diez principios, siete componentes y seis fases: Contextualizar, Recuperar, Interrogar, Someter a contraste, Organizar y Lograr transferencia. Su funcionamiento se representó en una secuencia demostrativa de cuatro sesiones para grado décimo, con seis evidencias observables. La comprobación conceptual mostró cobertura de las seis fases y los siete componentes; de nueve criterios funcionales, seis se cumplieron en el diseño, dos quedaron condicionados por el contexto institucional y uno —eficacia educativa— requiere aplicación con participantes. Se concluye que el aporte ofrece una arquitectura pedagógica trazable y adaptable, sin constituir todavía una validación empírica.

documents.abstract: The article examines digital monitoring of the implementation of strategic program documents of the Russian Federation and its connection to the evaluation of political and administrative decisions. It aims to identify the functions of modern information tools and the conditions for the managerial suitability of the data they gener-ate. The methods employed include normative analysis, functional comparison of government information systems, and qualitative document analysis. The research materials comprise legal acts, official publications of the Federal Treasury, and scholarly papers on public administration. Monitoring practices described in 2024 are compared with institutional changes introduced in 2026. The article identifies the distribution of functions be-tween the State Automated System “Upravlenie”, the State Integrated Information System “Electronic Budget”, and the state statistical platform within the unified plan for achieving national goals. It establishes the im-portance of accounting for the relationships between activities, indicators and national goal components, pre-serving the revision history, and documenting corrective action. The article proposes an analytical monitoring record, along with six criteria for the managerial suitability of monitoring, covering goal alignment, evidential support, temporal comparability, revision history, cross-system comparability, and completeness of response. The article also explores the conditions for verifying relationships and predictive signals derived with the use of artificial intelligence. The paper concludes that digital tools should be studied together with procedures for building evidence and using information within the competences of management participants.

Cities need land for homes, shops, roads, and public services. New construction changes that land. It can harm natural areas and water bodies, add to waste, and strain public services. NITI Aayog's 2021 report stated that 65% of 7,933 urban settlements in India had no master plan. That number tells us about planning coverage at the time. It does not tell us whether any single building was authorised. Artificial intelligence, which lets computers learn patterns from data, can help find physical changes by comparing satellite images taken on different dates. We test simple methods on two public datasets from outside India. First, we turn each image into a set of numbers using a pretrained neural network, a model already trained to recognise patterns in images. We feed those numbers to standard machine-learning classifiers that predict land categories and physical changes. The methods reach about 95 percent accuracy at spotting built-up land and about 83 percent accuracy at saying whether a small pair of images shows change, where each pair gets one label. We also train a small neural network on a standard change-detection benchmark. Separately, we run a preliminary descriptive check on an Agra sample of 48 patches, 7 of them positive. The results show that satellite images carry information about physical change. They do not show whether construction was planned or permitted.

Plant reflectance spectroscopy across the visible, near-infrared, and shortwave infrared domain encodes foliar biochemical and anatomical traits into contiguous spectral signatures with locally differentiable structure; however, extreme inter-band collinearity and unfavorable sample-to-feature ratios challenge predictive modeling. Conventional dimensionality reduction methods routinely adopted in spectroscopy, are column-permutation invariant: they treat adjacent wavelengths as unordered tabular columns and discard the sequential differential geometry of absorption features. Here, we propose Morpho-Spectral Projection Analysis (MSPA), a supervised dimensionality reduction operator that projects contiguous spectra into a compact morpho-spectral subspace through three complementary blocks: (i) additive continuum-removed absorption depth, area, and red-edge inflection kinematics; (ii) local multi-order singular eigenmodes (0th, 1st, and 2nd derivatives) partitioned across contiguous radiative sub-windows; and (iii) global Fisher-weighted canonical subspaces regularized via trace-normalized isotropic covariance shrinkage. We validated MSPA across 8,963 spectra spanning five plant systems, coupled with six classical machine learning classifiers and four Tabular Foundation Models (TabPFN v3, TabICL v2, TabDPT v1.2, and TabFM). Despite compressing the 1,580-band spectrum by 96%, MSPA outperformed the full spectrum in 92.0% of all benchmarks and conventional reducers in 90.0% of all model-crop evaluations, raising the global mean macro-F1 from 0.7756 (full spectrum) to 0.8520, accelerating in-context inference by up to 126.5x. Designed as a self-contained spectral projection operator, the MSPA method can be directly integrated into spectroscopy workflows via the open-source code available at GitHub: https://github.com/Lucas-Osco/mspa.

As the prevalence of chronic and communicable diseases increases, there has been an enhanced need for sensitive, rapid, reliable, and minimally invasive diagnostic technologies for monitoring disease progression and therapeutic effectiveness. Multifunctional nanomaterial-based electrochemical biosensors are emerging as powerful analytical tools due to their high sensitivity, selectivity, portability, and potential for real-time biomolecule detection. The purpose of this review is to shed light on the key underlying principles, nanomaterial engineering strategies, sensing principles, medical applications, and therapeutic assessment functionality of advanced electrochemical biosensors. Throughout the review, the merits of metallic nanoparticles, metal oxides, carbon nanotubes, graphene, MXenes, metal-organic frameworks, conducting polymers, and hybrid nanomaterials in increasing electrode conductivity, electroactive surface area, biomolecule immobilization, electron transfer kinetic, and electrochemical signal enhancement will be highlighted. This review delves deeper into the potential uses of sensors in identifying and tracking the processes of cancer, diseases of the cardiovascular system, diabetes, infections, problems in the nervous system, and cases of inflammation. It thoroughly discusses the role of drug monitoring, pharmacokinetics, and the potential uses of electrochemical sensors in providing ongoing monitoring of drugs in the human body. In addition, advancements in devices that are wearable and implantable, implement multiplexing, microfluidic principles, and artificial intelligence in biosensing are considered in the aspect of personal health and health care. Despite a multitude of technological improvements still present issues of biofouling, toxicity of nanomaterial, stability of biosensors, reproducibility, interference, calibration, mass production, and certification which makes it impossible to translate it into the practices of functional medicine.

Multimorbidity—the concurrent presence of two or more chronic long-term conditions—affects more than 37% of the global adult population and consumes 55%–80% of healthcare expenditure in high-income systems, yet artificial intelligence (AI) diagnostic systems remain overwhelmingly disease-specific, creating a profound structural mismatch with the multi-disease complexity characterizing the majority of real-world clinical encounters across twelve review-defined disease groups mapped to World Health Organization (WHO) ICD-11 chapters. This systematic review, following PRISMA 2020 and registered with OSF.IO (Registration DOI number: 10.17605/OSF.IO/3HZ45; Date of Registration: 25 October 2026), evaluated advanced AI technologies for simultaneous multi-domain disease detection and prediction. Nine electronic databases, PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Springer Link, Wiley, MDPI, and Google Scholar, were searched for peer-reviewed literature published from January 2015 to 31 August 2026. Database-specific Boolean searches (full strings in Supplementary Table S1 ) combined AI terms with terms for the twelve review-defined disease groups. Quality appraisal was done using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST tools (Cohen's κ = 0.84 refers to study screening agreement). Of 4,215 records identified (3,368 after removing 847 duplicates; 612 full texts assessed; 332 excluded), 280 studies met the eligibility criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis, and 185 provided quantitative performance data for a descriptive (non-pooled) synthesis. Deep learning models such as CNN, LSTM, ViT, and GNN reported high but heterogeneous discrimination across the twelve disease groups (AUC: 0.85–0.991). These values come from different tasks, datasets, and validation designs; they are not pooled estimates and do not show superiority of any architecture. Three of the highest-reporting single-disease studies (retrospective and not directly comparable) include: diabetic retinopathy detection (AUC 0.991; n = 128,175); cancer whole-slide image classification (AUC 0.98; n = 44,732); and cardiac arrhythmia detection (AUC 0.97; n = 91,232 ECGs). Convolutional neural networks were the most popular network type (26% of studies), while the main programming language was Python (68%). Three repeated gaps can be seen in the field of research in general, and those are: 1) lack of representation of people from developing countries in the training data; 2) scarce evidence from randomized prospective trials showing improved patient outcomes; and 3) an underdeveloped regulatory pathway for multi-disease AI as Software as a Medical Device (SaMD). Realizing simultaneous multi-disease AI at clinical scale demands five coordinated priorities: standardized cross-category benchmarks, demographically inclusive datasets with mandatory low- and middle-income country representation, prospective randomized trial validation, federated privacy-enhancing infrastructure designed to support GDPR, HIPAA, and DPDPA 2023 compliance (federated learning alone does not establish compliance), and internationally harmonized regulatory governance for multi-disease Software as a Medical Device authorization. Limitations of the review itself (English-only restriction, heterogeneity, overlapping public datasets, publication bias) are discussed in Section 8.5 . Systematic Review Registration: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/3HZ45

documents.abstract: The U.S. reproductive health landscape is fragmented, with legal, digital, and interpersonal privacy risks that are highly contextual and often poorly addressed by conventional privacy guidance. Prior work has proposed narrative threat modeling as an alternative to predominantly technical approaches to reproductive privacy communication. Building on this work, we introduce narrative threat zine-ing , a qualitative method that invites participants to communicate reproductive privacy through story and form rather than checklists or technical instruction. We report findings from four zine-making workshops in which participants created zines for people they worried about in the post- Roe landscape. Participants consistently framed reproductive privacy through relationships, lived experience, and storytelling, positioning zines as tools for awareness, solidarity, and collective sensemaking rather than prescriptive guidance. We argue that narrative threat zine-ing offers a method for examining how people interpret and communicate reproductive privacy under conditions of legal and social uncertainty.

Developing autonomous agents to deal with real-world problems is challenging, especially when developers are not necessarily specialists in artificial intelligence. Recent advances in machine learning for natural language processing tasks are reaching performance levels suitable for practical applications, although these approaches rely on opaque, inscrutable models. This poses three key challenges: the interface between the programming and the developer, the efficiency of the resulting agents, and the scrutiny of their behaviour. We tackle the challenge of developing autonomous agents over natural language environments in an efficient agent architecture that leverages recent developments in natural language processing and the intuitive folk psychology abstraction of the beliefs, desires, intentions (BDI) architecture. This paper introduces NatBDI , a new class of agent architecture that uses the BDI reasoning cycle with components driven by natural language processing. This allows a developer to instruct the agent more directly using a combination of controlled natural language structure and natural language knowledge as its programming interface. The resulting architecture handles natural language environments using a combination of language models and natural language inference to bootstrap the agent’s reasoning. We empirically assess the efficiency gains of this combination while introducing a more intuitively programmed autonomous agent. Instructions in this interface substantially improve agent performance in the experimental scenario over a baseline agent created using a pure machine learning approach. The resulting architecture shows that combining learned policies with intuitively engineered domain knowledge yields substantial performance gains. We expect this class of agents to provide a powerful, yet intuitive, tool for agent-driven programming.
