AI-generated review summaries are reshaping how consumers access product information, but their influence also extends to consumers who write reviews. Examining Amazon’s rollout of AI-generated review summaries, we find that these summaries encourage more review contributions and richer content. Consumers discuss product attributes absent from the summaries and elaborate on topics already covered. A controlled experiment suggests that summaries strengthen consumers’ belief that their contributions, together with others’, help future buyers make informed decisions. The increase in review contributions is stronger for products with many existing reviews or mixed ratings. Platform managers could prioritize summaries for products with mixed ratings, for which additional reviews can provide a more complete picture for future buyers. To build on richer review content, platforms could use writing prompts that highlight product attributes underrepresented in AI summaries. However, additional analyses suggest that AI summaries disproportionately benefit products that already sell well, potentially reinforcing sales concentration. Platforms could increase exposure for niche or new products, whereas policymakers could encourage fairness standards and periodic assessments of how AI-generated summaries affect product visibility and sales concentration. These findings highlight the potential of AI summaries to encourage consumer contributions, drawing attention to the risk of increased sales concentration.

This study examined how profiles of perceived teacher emotional support, helplessness, and self-efficacy for managing personal difficulties were associated with agentic engagement among Kuwaiti adult university students during wartime. Survey responses were collected from 546 students in higher education through a cross-sectional design. The stress measure referred to the wartime period and did not directly assess war exposure or trauma. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the measurement model. Latent profile analysis identified three profiles. These were Supported-Strained, Low-Support/Lower-Efficacy, and Low-Helplessness/High-Efficacy. Comparisons that accounted for classification uncertainty showed significantly lower agentic engagement in the Low-Support/Lower-Efficacy profile than in both other profiles. The Supported-Strained and Low-Helplessness/High-Efficacy profiles did not differ significantly in the primary analysis. After adjustment for gender, however, agentic engagement was significantly higher in the Supported-Strained profile. The findings suggest that agentic engagement during wartime differs across combinations of perceived support and psychological experiences. Greater helplessness did not consistently coincide with lower engagement. These cross-sectional associations do not establish that teacher support or wartime conditions caused the differences.

Comparisons of human and LLM persuasion usually report average attitude change. We reanalyse the Anthropic persuasion dataset (3,939 ratings of 1,313 arguments on 56 policy claims, written by people or by five Claude models) at the level of arguments, because each argument was rated three times. On average, Claude 3 Opus arguments shifted support by 0.48 Likert points and human arguments by 0.54; the difference was not significant (p = 0.37), and equivalence held only for a ±0.20 margin. The distributions differed sharply. Of 1,120 Claude arguments, 221 moved at least one reader away from the advocated position, against 1 of 174 human arguments. The gap appeared in 54 of the 56 claims (Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel p = 6 × 10-10), with matched starting attitudes and similar rates across all five models. We then asked whether word-level cues often recommended for persuasive and search-visible writing (statistics, research terms, certainty, inclusive language) explain either outcome. They did not predict negative shifts, their associations with average change largely disappeared once prompt type and initial attitude were controlled, and neither word lists nor a full bag-of-words model predicted change on unseen claims (out-of-fold R2 ≤ 0.003). In GEO-bench (4,996 Google top-five pages for 1,000 queries), the same cues varied little with rank and mainly reflected query intent. Average persuasion scores can hide frequent opposite-direction responses to LLM text, and these responses are not visible in simple word counts.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Characteristics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) severely restrict human control. This creates new challenges for socio-technical systems design especially in safety-critical domains, where control over risks is essential along with the accountability for any harm caused. Drawing from human factors and AI governance literature, expert interviews and participant observation in a complex high-risk AI use case from the railways, we developed ALIGN, a scenario-based method that supports the governance of and stakeholder involvement in AI development and implementation in three ways: raising awareness for potential accountability-control misalignments in socio-technical systems and their negative consequences, offering a structured approach to assessing the alignment between accountability and control for stakeholders in a given use case, and supporting effective design decisions to mitigate AI risks. We describe the iterative development and evaluation of ALIGN and discuss how this method promotes AI governance by highlighting the relevance of control-accountability alignment throughout the AI life cycle.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Who is accountable for what an AI system does, and how can that accountability be shown rather than asserted? Human sign-off and the autonomous agent both place the last word in a single party. Following a design science approach, we built and used a third arrangement, the verification interface: human, machine and an explicit ethics core form one construct, the core has the last word over both, and every output carries a tamper-evident receipt showing what was checked. The interface has been in daily use since February 2026 and had issued 12,398 receipts by 10 October 2026. In a sealed blind test on 1798 AI answers checked against company records, its verdicts matched the answer key in 97.1% of cases; a human check of 50 answers on which two AI auditors disagreed confirmed the answer key in 44. A check took a median of 1.9 s. We derive seven design requirements, report which the interface meets, and connect the approach to EU2122, a public content profile for receipts published as an IETF Internet-Draft. The economic hypothesis, that verification per output removes the review bottleneck of AI adoption and raises speed, quality and operating margin together, is stated but not tested. The interface assumes neither that AI is conscious nor that it has moral standing. All evidence comes from one system and is reported by its developer; it shows feasibility and measured accuracy in one domain, not effectiveness across organisations.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Nipple-sparing mastectomy (NSM) is increasingly performed in BRCA1/2 carriers, both for risk reduction and for treatment of breast cancer, but concern remains about glandular tissue left beneath the preserved nipple. We summarised the oncological outcomes of NSM in carriers. Methods: We searched PubMed/MEDLINE and Europe PubMed Central (Europe PMC) up to 30 September 2026, CENTRAL on 26 September 2026, and Embase on 7 November 2026 and screened the citations of relevant articles for series reporting outcomes of NSM in BRCA1/2 carriers. The outcomes were breast cancer diagnosed after risk-reducing NSM and locoregional recurrence after therapeutic NSM; cancers found at surgery were not counted. Proportions per woman were pooled with a binomial random-effects model (generalised linear mixed model, no continuity correction) and are reported as marginal (average-risk) and median-type (typical-study) proportions, with crude proportions, a beta-binomial model, follow-up strata, and approximate person-time analyses as checks. Two human reviewers went through all articles, with generative AI used only as an assistant, and the statistics were reviewed by a third author. Risk of bias was assessed with an adapted Joanna Briggs Institute checklist and certainty of evidence with GRADE. Results: Fifteen studies were included. After risk-reducing NSM, seven breast cancers occurred among 1215 women from eleven studies (crude proportion 0.58% (exact 95% CI 0.23–1.18%); model-based marginal proportion 0.60%, median-type 0.41% (95% CI 0.04–1.07%)); follow-up ranged from 33 to 129 months, and four of the seven cancers came from one international registry. After therapeutic NSM, locoregional recurrence occurred in 16 of 363 women from five studies (crude 4.4% (exact 95% CI 2.5–7.1%); model-based marginal proportion 4.3%, median-type 4.2% (95% CI 1.1–6.9%)); one study contributed 11 of the 16 events. Recurrence within the nipple–areolar complex was reported explicitly by only one study (none in 114 breasts). Sensitivity analyses yielded median-type proportions of 0.30% to 0.74% after risk-reducing NSM and 2.6% to 4.2% after therapeutic NSM. Risk of bias was moderate to high in most studies, and the certainty of the evidence was very low for both outcomes. Conclusions: In BRCA1/2 carriers, about 0.6% of women had breast cancer after risk-reducing NSM and about 4% had locoregional recurrence after therapeutic NSM, but follow-up was short and heterogeneous and the certainty of the evidence is very low. These data describe observed event frequencies and do not establish oncological safety or equivalence to other mastectomy techniques; longer prospective studies with time-to-event, gene-specific, and comparative reporting are needed.

This study aims to discuss and analyze the use of Languaging as a tool for linguistic construction in the teaching and learning process of Portuguese as a Heritage Language. The Languaging process is examined through Language-Related Episodes (LREs), understood as analytical tools for investigating learners’ linguistic reflection and for supporting pedagogical practices in heritage language education, more specifically in Portuguese. The study is based on the analysis of interactions that occurred in a Portuguese as a Heritage Language classroom context with participants living in South Africa, aged between 10 and 11. The main findings indicate that the LREs identified in the study are predominantly related to grammatical aspects and structural mechanisms of writing, and they highlight the crucial role of teacher mediation in learners’ cognitive engagement. The conclusions suggest that the use of Languaging in collaborative writing activities constitutes a powerful analytical and pedagogical tool for Portuguese as a Heritage Language instruction, as it promotes the articulation between form, meaning, and discourse, fostering interculturality in the classroom, while also underscoring the need for teacher education specifically focused on heritage language instruction and sensitive to the linguistic and sociocultural particularities of heritage speakers.

Low back pain (LBP) is a common occupational health problem among healthcare workers. While physical demands are known to contribute to LBP, few large-scale studies have investigated the contribution of psychosocial stressors. This study examined the association between occupational LBP and stress-related factors at a university hospital in Japan. In this cross-sectional study, we analyzed responses to the Brief Job Stress Questionnaire administered to 2,450 staff members. Participants were categorized into LBP and non-LBP groups. The prevalence of LBP and high stress was compared by occupation. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors independently associated with LBP. The overall prevalence of frequent LBP was 29.1%, being highest in nurses (39.3%) and lowest in doctors (11.1%). The odds ratio for LBP in nurses versus doctors was 3.54 (95% confidence interval 2.22–5.63). High stress status was more common in the LBP group than in the non-LBP group (25.1% versus 6.9%). Multivariate analysis showed that subjective physical workload, interpersonal stress in the workplace, physical fatigue, depressive symptoms, support from supervisors, work/life satisfaction, and body mass index were independently associated with LBP. These findings provide epidemiological evidence that both physical and psychosocial stressors are associated with occupational LBP among healthcare workers.

documents.abstract: Background Maintaining safe workplace environments in manufacturing industries is important for ensuring employees' health and maintaining effective production performance. Research on environmental safety and occupational health and safety is extensive, but the association between environmental safety and production efficiency and whether employees' safety knowledge supports this relationship, has received limited attention. Methods Data were collected from two independent cross-sectional purposive samples of footwear production workers (Wave 1 and Wave 2; N = 385 each), 3 months apart, and analyzed separately using Hayes PROCESS macro model 7 to investigate the indirect association between environmental safety and production efficiency through occupational health and safety, and the moderating effect of safety knowledge, with a simple slope test used to probe the interaction. Total effects were estimated using model 4. Results Contrary to the hypothesized direction, the association between environmental safety and occupational health and safety was weaker at higher safety knowledge in both waves; the interaction was significant after correction for multiple testing in Wave 1 only. In Wave 1, the interaction was a crossover: environmental safety was positively related to occupational health and safety only at low safety knowledge, and the indirect effect on production efficiency was significant only at low safety knowledge. The direct and total effects were not significant. In Wave 2, environmental safety was positively related to occupational health and safety at all levels of safety knowledge, with the association weakening as knowledge increased. The indirect effect was significant at low, mean and high safety knowledge, and the direct and total effects were also significant, indicating partial mediation. Conclusion In both waves, environmental safety was indirectly associated with production efficiency through occupational health and safety, at least among workers with lower safety knowledge, and this indirect association was weaker among workers with higher safety knowledge. These cross-sectional findings suggest that safe working environments may be particularly relevant for workers with lower safety knowledge.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Municipal solid waste workers operate in high-risk environments with limited institutional support, exposing them to diverse occupational hazards. This study explored occupational health and safety knowledge, practices, and experiences among municipal waste workers in Calabar, Nigeria, and examined the perceived impact of a health education intervention using a qualitative approach. A qualitative exploratory design was employed, involving Key Informant Interviews (KII) with 12 managers and Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) with 36 waste workers. Data were collected using semi-structured interview guides and analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings revealed low baseline knowledge of occupational hazards, poor safety practices, and systemic barriers such as inadequate provision of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), weak monitoring, funding constraints, and poor prioritization of worker health. The intervention improved awareness and perceived understanding of occupational hazards and safety practices, although structural barriers persisted. The study concludes that health education enhances knowledge but must be complemented by systemic reforms, including provision of PPE, enforcement of safety policies, and improved worker welfare.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Introduction Occupational health and safety (OHS) knowledge is important for identifying worker training needs and informing workplace injury prevention strategies. However, immigrant workers are often treated as a homogeneous group despite differences in settlement duration, residency status, and previous training experiences that may influence their knowledge of workplace rights, responsibilities, and safe work practices. This exploratory study examined differences in OHS knowledge among immigrants residing in Ontario for >5 years, immigrants residing in Ontario for ≤5 years, and Canadian-born construction workers in Ontario, Canada. Methods A cross-sectional survey of 206 construction workers assessed OHS knowledge using scenario-based questions developed with reference to Ontario OHS requirements. Associations between OHS knowledge scores and participant characteristics were examined using univariable analyses and a generalized linear model. Results Immigrants residing in Ontario for >5 years had higher OHS knowledge scores than immigrants residing in Ontario for ≤5 years. Knowledge also differed by residency status, with Canadian citizens born outside Canada and permanent residents scoring higher than Canadian-born and temporary-resident participants. In the adjusted model, longer residence in Ontario, residency status, and previous OHS training outside Ontario were significantly associated with higher OHS knowledge scores. Discussion The findings demonstrate that OHS knowledge cannot be adequately characterized through a simple immigrant/non-immigrant distinction. Differences associated with settlement duration, residency status, and previous training highlight important heterogeneity among construction workers and may help identify OHS educational and prevention needs. Future research should evaluate whether targeted interventions addressing these differences improve safety practices and occupational health outcomes.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The rapid evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) inference systems has led to significant improvements in serving efficiency. However, our systematic analysis reveals that current evaluation methodologies suffer from fundamental flaws that mask critical performance issues and impede scientific progress. Through a comprehensive examination of recent systems, we identify recurring pitfalls in evaluation practices across three key dimensions: Baseline Fairness, Evaluation Setup, and Metric Design. These pitfalls are uniquely problematic for LLM inference due to its dual-phase nature combining prefill and decode operations, heterogeneous workloads, and strict temporal requirements. We demonstrate how implementation differences frequently obscure algorithmic contributions, how workload selection often fails to represent production scenarios, and how metric normalization can hide substantial performance variability that directly impacts user experience. Traditional metrics derived from the classical machine learning serving setup fail to capture the autoregressive generation characteristics essential to LLM inference, leading to misleading conclusions about system performance. To address these challenges, we provide a comprehensive checklist of best practices and methodological recommendations for robust LLM inference evaluations. To demonstrate the practical application of our methodology, we present a case study of speculative decoding evaluation - a technique whose non-uniform token generation patterns with bursts during accepted predictions and delays during verification failures fundamentally confound conventional metrics. Our work establishes a rigorous foundation for evaluation methodology that can accelerate progress in LLM inference systems by ensuring meaningful comparisons, reproducible results, and metrics that reflect real-world requirements.

Large language models are increasingly used to create stories for children. Since bedtime stories can shape children's perceptions of social roles, this raises concerns about whether LLMs adapt narrative portrayals according to the intended recipient's gender. We conducted a large-scale study to examine gender stereotyping in LLM-generated bedtime stories. Using matched daughter/son prompts and a five-generation design, we analyze 62,873 retained stories from 16 LLMs across 35 country settings and 12 narrator roles. We introduce a multi-level evaluation framework combining context-adjusted lexical rate contrasts, relative stereotype alignment, narrator-recipient interaction analysis, human evaluation, and representation-level interventions to examine both the consistency and interpretability of these differences. Our results reveal systematic differences in narrative framing: son-directed stories emphasize higher agency and lower communion compared to daughter-directed stories. While narrator gender expresses limited moderation on these patterns, high sociability exhibits a more pronounced interaction. Human evaluations demonstrate consistent agreement, although correspondence with lexical measures varies across narrative dimensions. Additionally, hidden-state analyses reveal decodable recipient-gender information. These findings demonstrate persistent yet context-dependent representational disparities in LLM-generated children's stories and motivate narrative-specific bias evaluation beyond short-form benchmarks.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Current diabetic retinopathy management relies primarily on contemporaneous severity grading and does not directly quantify the short-term risk of vision-threatening complications. We developed and internally evaluated image-based artificial intelligence models for one-year prediction of diabetic retinopathy severity, proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) and center-involved diabetic macular edema (ci-DME) using retinal imaging acquired during routine care.The prospective multicenter EviRed cohort included 3,183 patients with diabetes, 8,520 visits and 16,509 eye-level observations collected across 14 French hospitals. Device-specific ensembles were developed for ultra-widefield color fundus photography (CLARUS500 and OPTOS) and OCT angiography (CIRRUS5000 and PLEX Elite9000). Predictions from individual images and both eyes were aggregated at the patient-visit level. Participants were partitioned at the patient level into adevelopment set (65\%) and a held-out test set (35\%).For prediction of diabetic retinopathy severity at the subsequent annual visit, OPTOS and CLARUS500 achieved quadratic weighted kappa values of 0.866 (95\% confidence interval, 0.842--0.878) and 0.852 (0.830--0.877), respectively. For incident ci-DME, CIRRUS5000 achieved the highest discrimination (AUC, 0.826; 0.770--0.878), whereas PLEX Elite9000 yielded the highest AUC point estimate for incident PDR (0.877; 0.807--0.950). Late fusion did not consistently outperform the strongest device-specific model. In secondary complete-case analyses, observed ci-DME incidence increased across quartiles of the image-derived risk score, reaching 19.7--30.4\% in the highest-risk quartile. AI models also achieved higher AUC point estimates than unassisted expert risk assessments for both complications, although these comparisons were exploratory.Retinal imaging acquired at a single routine-care visit therefore contains information associated with diabetic retinopathy severity and vision-threatening complications one year later. These findings support image-based short-term risk stratification, while external validation, calibration and prospective clinical utility assessment remain necessary before deployment.

Background. Ambient clinical AI — software that listens to a consultation and drafts the clinical note, often called an AI scribe — is now a flagship use of artificial intelligence in healthcare. Most tools delivering it are proprietary and cloud-based: consultation audio leaves the building, errors cannot be independently characterised, and the clinician who signs the note answers for output nobody outside the vendor can examine. Open, fully local alternatives that a clinician or researcher can inspect, run and modify remain rare. Objective. This paper reports OpenConsult, an open-source AI scribe with live clinical decision support that runs entirely on one machine in the consulting room and is inspectable end to end, and describes its formative evaluation. Methods. Evaluation was formative and used synthetic consultations only (scripted and acted). Automated tests ran fifteen scripted consultations with pre-written marking schemes, checking transcription quality gates, the urgency alarm’s behaviour across emergency and routine scripts, and whether every cited claim in a note points to a real transcript line. Five acted consultations followed in a real consulting room, and the AI assistants that built the system ran an adversarial security audit under the developer’s direction. The work is reported against the applicable DECIDE-AI items, one stage before live clinical evaluation. Results. OpenConsult is a fully local, open-source consultation assistant, built by a practising general practitioner directing AI coding assistants, running on a single consumer graphics card. It transcribes the consultation live and separates the speakers, drafts a structured clinical note with every sentence linked to its supporting transcript words, runs live decision support whose urgency alarm is shown only to the doctor, drafts referral letters, and offers a supervised spoken history-taking mode. In generated notes, 301 of 302 citations pointed to real transcript lines — an existence check, with clinical faithfulness unmeasured pending independent rating; the one uncited claim was flagged for manual checking. The urgency alarm fired in all eight scripted emergencies and stayed silent in six of seven routine consultations. Five acted consultations surfaced five defects the automated checks had missed, four of them serious; all were fixed, each pinned by a regression test. The security audit returned twelve findings, including one critical vulnerability, fixed and verified before any public exposure. Conclusions. OpenConsult is a working, auditable proof of concept — not yet a validated clinical tool — released for research and education only, with real patient care out of scope. It is intended as an open research instrument: it records whether the reviewing clinician opened the cited evidence before approving, how long review takes, and every revision of its decision support, making human review of ambient clinical AI measurable. Independent, prospective evaluation is required before any step toward care.

documents.abstract: Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. We introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning. Within this framework, agents autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire new capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. OpenKAGE builds on two key mechanisms: (1) a two-layer knowledge representation, with a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills that retains the applicability conditions needed for reuse; and (2) a knowledge-sharing mechanism that semantically consolidates textual experience into a continuously evolving shared knowledge graph, while executable skills are shared verbatim. In Minecraft, OpenKAGE supports open-ended lifelong learning, enabling agent groups to sustain exploration and reach advanced technological milestones. Furthermore, the accumulated knowledge can be transferred to a newly initialized agent group on a different backbone model, improving its survival and exploration progress.

Artificial intelligence is entering the everyday work of secondary schools. Teachers encounter AI-based tools both in classroom organisation and in feedback or adaptation tasks. As these tools become more visible in school practice, their educational role and practical value need to be examined in relation to the conditions of real classrooms. This is especially relevant in classes with varied learning characteristics, where students differ in pace and readiness to participate. In these settings, AI may help teachers adapt instructional material and provide more individualised support. Its value, however, depends on professional judgement and on how each tool is connected to pedagogical purpose. This paper examines opportunities and challenges related to the use of artificial intelligence in secondary education. The planned study will use teachers’ accounts to examine how AI tools are understood and used in secondary school practice. It is designed as a qualitative inquiry based on semi-structured interviews with secondary education teachers, with the interview material examined thematically. Through teachers’ accounts, the study will explore how AI is understood in relation to lesson preparation and student support, while also examining what makes its use difficult in day-to-day teaching. The paper approaches AI as a tool whose usefulness depends on classroom context and teachers’ pedagogical decisions.

documents.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) are moving from experimental demonstrations to operational tools in military aviation. This article examines the main opportunities these technologies offer in six areas: immersive flight and mission training, cockpit and helmet-mounted displays, live-virtual-constructive training, aircraft maintenance, mission planning and debriefing, and human-performance training. Using an analytical review of academic and professional literature, the study compares the potential benefits of each application area with its principal technical and human-factors limitations. The findings show that VR offers the clearest near-term value in cost-effective procedural and tactical training, while AR offers the greatest long-term value in airborne information display and in maintenance support. Simulator sickness, latency, registration accuracy, cybersecurity and the need for validated transfer-of-training evidence remain the key barriers. The article concludes with practical recommendations for armed forces and military education institutions that wish to adopt these technologies in a phased and evidence-based way.

Urban biodiversity loss is increasingly framed as a governance challenge with intertwined ecological and social dimensions, yet little is known about who participates in local biodiversity planning, what authority that participation carries, and whether plans recognize and address disproportionate harms. This study presents the first comparative analysis at this scale of participation in Local Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (LBSAPs), examining 98 plans from 98 municipalities across 26 countries. Using a hybrid methodology combining large language model-assisted verbatim extraction with manual coding (96.4% extraction accuracy), plans were assessed across four dimensions: participant recognition, participatory mechanisms, authorship, and transparency. Of the 98 plans, 71 (72%) documented some participatory mechanism, but only 18 (18%) granted participants any authority over plan content, and only 2 (2%) shared control over resources. Authorship was concentrated in city governments (93 of 98 plans), and 39 cities (40%) provided no transparency about participatory processes. Knowledge-holder positioning was dominated by scientists (M = 0.60 on a 0–1 scale) while Indigenous peoples (M = 0.08), marginalized groups (M = 0.01), and youth (M = 0.03) were systematically excluded. A distributive analysis revealed a marginalized-specific redress gap: 16 plans recognized marginalized groups as bearing environmental harm, but only 4 of those plans offered programmatic response; a 75% recognition-without-remedy rate not seen for any other actor type. These findings indicate that prevailing LBSAP governance architectures may constrain conservation effectiveness, by excluding the situated knowledge of communities most affected by biodiversity loss, and may reproduce environmental injustice, by acknowledging disproportionate harms without acting on them. Governance reforms that meaningfully redistribute participatory authority are needed to advance both biodiversity outcomes and equitable urban conservation.

Plant genomics with a hybrid classical-quantum model Artificial intelligence and quantum computing for the digital design of plant genomes Italian patent application no. 102026000034324, filed on 18 November 2026. Inventor, applicant and sole rights holder: Paolo Ciccolella. This invention proposes combining artificial intelligence and quantum computing to explore possible combinations of plant DNA and identify those worth investigating further. For businesses interested in plant genomics, the idea is to provide early guidance for computational design: turning a vast number of possibilities into selected, evaluated and documented digital candidates. The challenge is easy to picture. If DNA is a large instruction book, studying alternative versions of some passages means comparing many combinations. Three alternatives for each of twenty regions already produce more than three billion possibilities. The method tackles this complexity by dividing the work between a classical computer, two AI models and a quantum search component. HOW THE HYBRID MODEL WORKS The idea is to choose one alternative for each DNA region being studied, put the choices together and evaluate the resulting combination. Everything happens on a computer. The process follows six steps. • Prepare the data. The computer starts with a digital version of the plant’s DNA, called a reference genome. It identifies the regions to study and organises the available alternative sequences for each one, recording where they come from. • Give each alternative an initial score. The first AI model examines each alternative separately. Having learned from other cases, it can provide guidance before any complete combination in the new case has been evaluated. The computer also measures similarity between the ends of sequences that will be placed next to one another. These scores and measurements define the selection problem. [B12] • Search for combinations. The quantum component receives this problem expressed in numbers. It uses QAOA, an algorithm whose role is to propose combinations while seeking to favour those with better scores. Qubits represent the possible choices; the DNA sequences remain on the classical computer, which sets and updates the algorithm’s parameters. [B11] • Evaluate the whole combination. The computer checks that each combination selects exactly one alternative per region and assembles valid choices into a digital candidate. The second AI model evaluates the complete candidate, including relationships between its parts that the first AI model could not observe when examining them separately. • Guide the next search. The system compares the overall evaluation with the score predicted at the start and uses the difference to update the search. When only a few results are available, it limits the correction’s influence to avoid relying too heavily on sparse information. • Return verifiable proposals. For each selected candidate, the system retains the chosen sequences, their provenance and the evaluations performed. It also records a digital fingerprint, a code used to check the content. Researchers can reconstruct the proposal and understand how it was selected. If necessary data are missing, the system flags this. A concrete example: the patent uses the digital reference for Micro-Tom tomato and considers three regions, each with three alternatives created for the test. There are 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 possible combinations. The search uses a nine-qubit quantum circuit simulated on a classical computer. This tests the computational method without producing plants. [B14] INDUSTRIAL APPLICATIONS The patent describes the production of verifiable digital representations of candidate genomes. Its industrial role lies in designing and selecting hypotheses, ahead of experimental work. Applications across sectors require data and models suited to the objectives under study. • NGT and assisted evolution techniques. NGTs, or new genomic techniques, include approaches known in Italy as TEA, meaning assisted evolution techniques, which enable targeted changes to genetic material. The proposed method could support research by comparing genomic hypotheses before experimental work. For seed and biotechnology companies, the prospect is to build a reasoned set of digital candidates for further investigation within NGT/TEA programmes. • Seed industry and variety development. For seed companies and research teams, the method could support the preliminary selection of combinations for further study. Research objectives could include drought or salinity tolerance, disease resistance and yield stability. Its contribution would be to establish research priorities while preserving the reasoning behind them. • Fresh produce and food processing. Computational design could focus on commercial characteristics such as product quality, shelf life and processing suitability. Tomato, pepper and aubergine are examples of supply chains that future projects could address, connecting growers’ and processors’ needs with the criteria used to evaluate candidates. • Nutraceuticals and plant ingredients. One possible development concerns plants of interest for functional ingredients, extracts and bioactive compounds. The method could explore genomic combinations in programmes focused, for example, on pigments or plant metabolites, providing documented candidates to guide subsequent analysis. • Plant biotechnology and industrial raw materials. For crops intended for oils, fibres or biomass, the method could help compare genomic hypotheses against supply chain objectives. Reconstructible digital records would support information exchange between teams developing the models and those planning subsequent experimental work. • Bioinformatics and computing centres. The most direct application is within the information systems of laboratories, computing centres and plant genomics businesses. The process could underpin software modules or analytical services that explore combinations and return candidates with scores and execution logs, integrating quantum search into the workflow. Introduction As part of a strategy to increase magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) capacity, the UK government funded the purchase of manufacturer artificial intelligence (AI) MRI image reconstruction software on MRI scanners. It aimed to reduce scan duration without compromising image quality and has been widely installed on clinical MRI scanners across the UK. Methods This is a mixed methods study, using an initial questionnaire to quantify opinions followed by focus groups of responders to further explore their views on technical issues. Patient views on the use of AI in MRI image reconstruction for reducing acquisition times, and more generally in their MRI pathway, were assessed. Results Study participants prefer improved image quality over faster acquisition times. If reducing acquisition times with AI, they feel it should only be used if extremely accurate images can be ascertained. They are uncomfortable with the use of manufacturer AI software for image reconstruction where accuracy is not stated and would like to be told about the use of AI in MRI. Conclusions Many participants felt that manufacturer AI software for MRI image reconstruction may be used only if a high accuracy is demonstrated, and if the training data is representative of the patient population, to not exacerbate health inequalities. This information is not currently given by manufacturers, which made the patient representatives concerned. Implication for practice •Local validation of AI image reconstruction software may make patients more confident about its use. •AI patient information materials should be accessible and discuss accuracy, and radiographers can be trained to help inform and reassure patients. •Engagement with all clinical stakeholders in MRI should be undertaken to understand their views on AI, and how manufacturer AI software should be implemented.

documents.abstract: Academic stress among university students is commonly linked to heavy assignment loads, yet the role of time management in this relationship remains contested. This study examines the effects of assignment workload and time management on academic stress and tests time management as a moderator. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among active students of Universitas Pamulang, Indonesia (n = 37, purposive sampling) using a five-point Likert questionnaire, and analysed with multiple regression and moderated regression. Assignment workload had a positive and significant effect on academic stress (β = 0.734, p < .001), whereas time management had no direct effect once workload was controlled (β = 0.081, p = .552). The model explained 62.0% of the variance in academic stress. Time management significantly weakened the workload–stress relationship (interaction b = −0.308, p = .002, ΔR² = .095). The study positions time management as a buffer rather than a direct predictor. Universities should combine coordinated scheduling of assignments with proactive time-management support.

Over the past decade, the innovative convergence of cloud computing, natural language processing (NLP), and large language models (LLM) has triggered a paradigm shift in human-computer interaction. This study aims to conceptually review and propose a research design to objectively analyze the effect of security and privacy perceptions on the use of AI as a venting medium. The proposed method is a conceptual quantitative research design with a correlational approach, planned for Generation Z respondents. Based on a literature synthesis of referenced studies, the findings indicate a highly significant positive correlation between dispositional shame and self-disclosure to artificial intelligence (r = 0.337, p < 0.001, n = 182). The conceptual review concludes that AI operates effectively as a complementary screening instrument but risks triggering an atrophy of social resilience, thus necessitating juridical protection through the Personal Data Protection Law (UU PDP).

documents.abstract: Amaç: Bu çalışma, insan merkezli bakım ile işgücü refahı, hasta güvenliği ve sağlık hizmetlerinde kalite yönetimi arasındaki kavramsal bağlantıları aydınlatmak ve insan merkezli kalite yönetişiminin kavramsal bir modelini geliştirmek amacıyla ISO 7101:2023 standardına yönelik nitel bir belge analizi yapmayı amaçlamıştır. Yöntemler: Çalışmada, Bowen’ın (2009) belge analizi çerçevesine göre nitel kavramsal belge analizi ilkeleri uygulanmıştır. Yöntemler: ISO 7101:2023 standardının 4 ila 10. maddelerinin (kuruluş bağlamı, liderlik, planlama, destek, operasyon, performans değerlendirmesi ve iyileştirme) içerik analizi ve her maddeyle ilgili ifadelerin ilk kodlaması, ardından kodların mantıksal tematik gruplandırılması gerçekleştirilmiştir. Sonuçlar: Altı tema ortaya çıkmıştır: kalite yönetiminin insan merkezli dönüşümü; hizmet kullanıcı deneyimi ve ortak üretim; şefkatli bakım, etik ve kapsayıcılık; işgücü refahı ve sürdürülebilir kalite; hasta güvenliği ve risk kültürü; performans değerlendirmesi ve sürekli iyileştirme. Bulgular: ISO 7101:2023, mevzuata uygunluk ve denetimin ötesine geçen, ilişkisel, etik ve insan merkezli bir düzeyde kavramsal bir çerçeve sunmaktadır. Sonuç: Bulgularımıza dayanarak, sürekli bir döngü içinde uygulanan altı birbirine bağlı boyuttan oluşan “İnsan Odaklı Kalite Yönetişim Modeli”ni öneriyoruz: liderlik ve kalite kültürü, risk temelli düşünme ve etik yönetişim, işgücü refahı ve psikolojik güvenlik, insan odaklı bakım ve ortak üretim, hasta güvenliği ve hizmet kullanıcı deneyimi ile performans değerlendirmesi ve sürekli iyileştirme. Bu çalışma, sağlık hizmetleri kalite yönetimi, hasta güvenliği ve işgücü refahı üzerine mevcut literatüre insan merkezli ve etik bir kalite yönetişim perspektifi sunmakta ve sağlık kuruluşlarının kalite uygulamalarının ISO 7101:2023 standardına uymasına yardımcı olacak bir kavramsal çerçeve sağlamaktadır.Anahtar kelimeler: ISO 7101:2023; sağlık hizmetleri kalite yönetimi; insan merkezli bakım; işgücü refahı; hasta güvenliği; belge analizi; kalite yönetişimi.

Digital inclusion with generative AI depends not only on educators’ access to tools but on how they use them. Comparing the benefits educators perceive with the uses they report may reveal gaps between what educators believe AI can do and how they use it in teaching. In this exploratory secondary analysis of survey data from 293 Minnesota PK-12 and higher education educators, we compared endorsement of improved accessibility for diverse learners as a benefit of generative AI with reported use of AI to enhance accessibility for students with disabilities. Because the items differ in scope and target population, the comparison describes response proportions, not a failure to act on a belief. Among 160 AI-using educators who answered both items, 133 (83.1%) endorsed the benefit and 51 (31.9%) reported the use (McNemar exact p < 0.001). Subgroup differences were not detected, though power was limited. Among all AI users, self-rated competence was associated with reported accessibility use (44.0% vs. 27.9%; adjusted OR = 2.31, 95% CI [1.13, 4.73]); among endorsers, the estimate was imprecise. Keyword-selected open-ended responses more often described general differentiation and language support than disability-specific use. We discuss measurement implications and propose supports as hypotheses for evaluation.

Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in medical training, but evidence from African residency programs is scarce. We assessed how internal medicine residents in Ethiopia use GenAI and how they perceive its impact on clinical learning and clinical decision-making. Methods We conducted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study consisting of a national cross-sectional online survey of internal medicine residents (June to August 2026), followed by two focus group discussions (FGDs) with 10 residents at two universities (September 2026) to explain the survey findings. Perceived impact was measured with five-point Likert items and two composite scores (learning, five items; decision-making, eight items). Associations with frequency of use were tested with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. FGD data were organized deductively into categories based on the survey topics. Results Of 252 respondents from 18 institutions, 98.8% had used GenAI and 75.4% used it daily; ChatGPT was used by 91.6% of users. The mean composite score for perceived impact on clinical learning was 3.83 out of 5 (70.7% high) and for clinical decision-making 3.86 out of 5 (67.7% high). Agreement was highest for improved differential diagnosis (90.8%), learning efficiency (81.9%) and support for self-directed learning (79.5%), and lowest for ward-round performance (64.3%) and confidence in complex cases (71.4%). Daily use was more frequent among residents with more than three hours of daily internet use (82.3% versus 66.7% to 67.4%; p = 0.024) and was not associated with age, sex, marital status, year of residency, device access or formal training. In the FGDs, residents described GenAI as a fast, supportive tool for learning and clinical work, as an aid to reasoning and not a replacement for physician judgment, and as a possible threat to independent learning. Conclusions Residents perceive GenAI as helpful for self-directed learning and diagnostic reasoning while keeping final responsibility for clinical decisions. These findings reflect perceptions and not measured outcomes, so objective evaluation of its effects on learning and clinical performance is needed.

documents.abstract: Introduction and aims To evaluate the authenticity detection performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) using real and AI-generated intraoral photographs and to compare their performance with human evaluators with different levels of dental experience. Methods A dataset of 1,000 intraoral photographs (500 real and 500 AI-generated) across 5 standardised views was constructed from single-institution clinical images and the publicly available AI-Hub dataset. GPT-5.1 (OpenAI), Claude Opus 4.5 (Anthropic), and Gemini 3.0 Pro (Google) evaluated all images through vendor APIs. Human evaluation was conducted using a stratified random subset of 200 images by fourth-year dental students, dentists with ≤5 years, and dentists with ≥6 years of clinical experience (n = 5 per group). Results In the 200-image subset, dentists with ≥6 years showed the highest performance (accuracy: 0.740; F1-score: 0.675), followed by dentists with ≤5 years (accuracy: 0.690; F1-score: 0.557). Across the 1,000-image dataset, GPT-5.1 achieved the highest performance among the MLLMs (accuracy: 0.646; F1-score: 0.452), whereas Claude Opus 4.5 showed the lowest (accuracy: 0.571; F1-score: 0.249). All groups demonstrated substantially higher accuracy for real images than for the curated, visually plausible AI-generated images, with the MLLMs combining near-perfect specificity (0.998-1.000) and low recall (0.142-0.292), whereas human specificity was 0.890-0.990 and recall 0.390-0.540. The mandibular occlusal view showed the lowest accuracy among the MLLM groups. Conclusion Current MLLMs showed lower performance than experienced human evaluator panels, with limited recall for the AI-generated images in this study, suggesting that they are not yet suitable as standalone authenticity detection tools in dentistry. Clinical Relevance The increasing visual realism of generative artificial intelligence-generated intraoral photographs suggests that authenticity cannot be judged from visual inspection alone, and robust validation is needed before such images are used as clinical records, teaching material, or training data for artificial intelligence.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has altered how assessment supports learning and evidences achievement in higher education. Early institutional responses concentrated on academic integrity, detection, and task redesign, while a rapidly expanding empirical literature documents the contingent benefits and trade-offs of AI-mediated learning. This conceptual paper develops an assessment-specific framework organised around two dimensions: the distribution of learning-relevant cognitive responsibility and the visibility of student process. GenAI can operate as an engagement amplifier when it supports cognitive and metacognitive activity while preserving student responsibility for the intellectual work that matters, or as a cognitive substitute when it displaces that work while enabling successful task completion. The framework distinguishes immediate AI-supported performance from durable capability, whether demonstrated independently or with GenAI, and connects this distinction to the validity of inferences drawn from assessment evidence. Rather than proposing a universal solution to what has been called the wicked problem of AI and assessment, the framework offers an evaluative lens for judging how particular assessment configurations distribute cognitive responsibility and make student thinking visible, and whether the resulting evidence can support defensible claims about achievement. This reframing informs assessment judgements without prescribing a single model for all higher education contexts.

As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in news production, journalistic credibility can no longer be understood only through audience trust in machine-generated content. This article examines how AI-generated and AI-assisted journalism is made to appear trustworthy through textual, editorial, and institutional cues. Drawing on qualitative comparative content analysis of a 37-text corpus comprising 14 AI-generated or AI-assisted news articles, 14 human-written comparison articles, four newsroom AI policy documents, and five correction or controversy-related texts, the study analyses how credibility is constructed through authorship, disclosure, sourcing, human oversight, correction practice, and institutional framing. The findings show that AI-assisted journalism can reproduce familiar signs of professional news, including factual tone, structured formats, institutional attribution, and data specificity. Yet these cues do not necessarily make editorial responsibility visible. The article develops the concept of algorithmic credibility performance to explain how AI journalism assembles trustworthiness through uneven arrangements of transparency, evidence, and accountability before audiences respond.

documents.abstract: Background: The clinical relevance of routinely available peripheral inflammatory indices in major depressive disorder (MDD) remains uncertain, particularly regarding recent suicide attempts, depressive symptom severity, and their discriminative performance. This study investigated these associations using conventional statistical analyses and explainable machine learning. Methods: This retrospective, single-center study included 86 patients with MDD and 80 healthy controls. Six blood-derived inflammatory indices were examined for between-group differences and associations with recent suicide attempts and depressive symptom severity. Individual-marker discrimination was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis, while three ensemble machine-learning models were evaluated using nested cross-validation and compared with MHR alone. Explainable artificial intelligence methods were applied to interpret model predictions. Results: Patients with MDD showed higher MHR, NHR, SIRI, and AISI values than controls. Recent suicide attempts were associated with higher SII, SIRI, and AISI, and these associations persisted after adjustment for age and sex; lower LHR was observed only in the unadjusted comparison and was not significant after adjustment. No inflammatory index was significantly associated with depressive symptom severity. MHR demonstrated the strongest individual discrimination. Machine-learning models showed modest discriminative performance without clear improvement over MHR alone, and feature-importance analyses consistently highlighted MHR. Conclusions: Here we show that peripheral inflammatory indices exhibit distinct observational associations with MDD and recent suicidal behavior. However, their diagnostic and predictive clinical utility remains unestablished and requires prospective, adequately controlled, independently validated studies.

This conceptual paper introduces Persistent Records Without Decoding Support, a mechanism by which a record outlasts the conventions, skills, or equipment needed to read it. The paper distinguishes two requirements for practical access. Recoverability concerns whether a reader can extract the marks or data. Intelligibility concerns whether the reader can establish what they mean. Each depends on the support available to a particular reader at a particular time. The documented case is the decipherment of Linear B. Clay tablets from Knossos and Pylos preserved palace accounts for more than 3,000 years. Before decipherment, scholars could copy the signs and recognize some pictured objects while the words beside them remained unreadable. Building on work by Alice Kober and Emmett Bennett, Michael Ventris identified the language as an early form of Greek in 1952. A tablet discovered later at Pylos helped confirm the reading. The words for two tripods appeared beside a tripod sign and the numeral 2. The 1986 BBC Domesday Project provides a contrast. By 2002, few working systems could read its videodiscs. A surviving drive supplied data for the CAMiLEON emulation demonstration, and preservation teams carried material onto newer systems. Access had become precarious while the means of reading still existed. The paper places this case alongside Jeff Rothenberg’s account of digital obsolescence and his proposal to emulate older computers. Part of the Records and Circulation series within On Human Modeling, the paper also offers a distinction relevant to human–AI interaction. An archive might preserve an AI system’s responses as sequences of token IDs. A later reader could copy every number, yet recovering the wording would depend on finding or reconstructing the mapping from those numbers to text.

This article presents findings from the evaluation of a digital literacy pilot programme for men leaving prison Tech4PrisonLeavers. It has been recognised that people leaving prison may need digital skills to support their reintegration into society. The literature on technology and digital skills programmes in the criminal justice system has largely focused on digital elements rather than human and interpersonal elements.Based on interviews with programme volunteers and coordinators, this article argues that the human factor is a key element in digital literacy programmes for prison leavers. While the digital elements of the pilot were pivotal too, the human factor represented in this case by the volunteer mentors, the volunteer-participant relationship, and associated person-centred approaches is central to supporting prison leavers’ digital needs. These interactions may ultimately lead to a two-way humanisation process in which mentors debunk prison stereotypes and the participants demystify professionals and the digital world.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the way learners look for information, develop ideas, and complete assignments, which makes it necessary to rethink what independent thinking means. Drawing on the philosophy of education, including Islamic educational philosophy, this article addresses three questions: the nature of learners’ independent thinking, the duality of AI as either a reinforcer of reasoning or a source of intellectual dependency, and the reconfiguration of educators’ roles and learning objectives. The study is a qualitative, descriptive-critical literature review of eleven Indonesian-language journal articles published between 2023 and 2026, supported by foundational theoretical and philosophical works. It argues that AI’s effect on reasoning is not an inherent property of the technology; rather, it is likely to be shaped by the cognitive operations handed over to the machine and by the order in which AI is introduced into a learning task. Dependency is most likely when AI takes over analysis and judgment, and least likely when it is used to explain or to test the learner’s own thinking. Educators are therefore urged to design thinking processes, move assessment from products to processes, and nurture scholarly ethics such as honesty and tabayyun (careful verification). These conclusions are conceptual and call for empirical testing across educational levels.

Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). Model developers use the attacks discovered during internal red-teaming to harden agents through adversarial training before deployment, a collaborative offensive-defensive process known in cybersecurity as purple-teaming. However, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee robustness gains from subsequent adversarial training. Specifically, we find that two state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, suffer from mode collapse, repeatedly discovering similar attack strategies whose additional successes add no additional robustness improvements to adversarial training. To address this gap, we introduce PIPETTE, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that effectively converts red-teaming discoveries into defender robustness improvements. PIPETTE employs a dictionary learning-based reward that encourages broader coverage of attack strategies during red-teaming. It also integrates an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to IPI defense, enabling agents to resist attacks while completing legitimate user tasks. Extensive evaluations across agentic benchmarks (AgentDojo and ASB) demonstrate that PIPETTE produces defenders that achieve near-zero attack success rates on static attacks and can withstand strong adaptive attacks, while maintaining benign task utility close to that of the undefended baseline.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable high-capacity large language models (LLMs) with high sparse computation, making them attractive for deployment on private hardware. However, distributing model weights exposes valuable intellectual property (IP) to leakage and unauthorized redistribution, creating an urgent need to both verify model ownership and trace leaked copies to individual licensees. Existing model-watermarking techniques are ill-suited for meeting this need because they are fragile under MoE's dynamic routing or require costly retraining to embed a distinct watermark for each licensee, thus making scalable distribution difficult. To address these challenges, we present PPMoE, the first plug-and-play multi-licensee watermarking framework for MoE LLMs. Rather than training a separate model per user, PPMoE trains a compact set of mergeable incremental weight modules that steer the MoE router toward distinct, mutually compatible routing patterns. During model distribution, the model owner selectively merges unique combinations of these pre-trained, mutually compatible modules into the base model on the fly, embedding a licensee-specific watermark without additional training. PPMoE supports reliable multi-licensee attribution under both white- and black-box threat models. In the white-box setting, attribution is done by inspecting triggered routing decisions or the merged weight modules responsible for these decisions, whereas in the black-box setting, attribution relies on analyzing output token likelihood ratios. Extensive experiments across five state-of-the-art MoE models, seven benchmark datasets, and varying number of licensees show that PPMoE achieves very high attribution accuracy while preserving base model utility and maintaining strong robustness to various adaptive watermark-removal attacks.

documents.abstract: While popular operating systems such as Linux and Windows were originally designed as monolithic kernels, an increasing number of kernel subsystems have become extensible using eBPF. Users can now define custom policies for essential kernel mechanisms, such as the process scheduler, page cache, and network stack, without recompiling the kernel. These mechanisms give developers significant freedom to fit the kernel to their applications' workloads, but the question of which policy to deploy remains open. We study how to use agentic AI to automate kernel policy development, selection, and deployment, focusing on the page cache and the process scheduler as two representative subsystems. We show that existing approaches fall short: evolutionary and agentic search runs offline, is relatively expensive, and often fails to generalize to online workloads, while online knob tuners are encumbered by the knobs' lack of expressivity. In contrast, we propose Polymorph, which learns online: an AI agent writes a generalized, granular policy once, and a user mode tuner adjusts its parameters during runtime, with no LLM in the loop. For the page cache, Polymorph improves throughput over Linux's LRU by 8.4% on unseen data, nearly twice the gain of the best existing policy, while adapting to workload changes at runtime and costing only 16M tokens once, versus 125-240M tokens per workload for agentic offline search. For the process scheduler, it improves on Linux's default by 2.75x across six workloads, versus 2.27x for the best fixed sched_ext policy.

Abstract Dynamic Modulus (DM) is a critical characteristic for the design of Hot Mix Asphalt (HMA), which is currently determined through complex empirical models. This study applies advanced explainable Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques to predict DM, enhance the understanding of the factors affecting it, and support design optimization applications. An extensive experimental dataset was used that included a variety of aggregate gradations, different types of bituminous binders, volumetric characteristics, and test conditions in terms of test temperature and loading rate. Eight different predictive models were developed, ranging from simple linear regression to advanced machine learning models, including Support Vector Machines (SVM) and ensemble techniques, using a random selection scheme for cross-validation. Comparison of model performance indicated that the best performing model was the Cubic SVM, with an R 2 = 0.96 and RMSE = 2.22 × 10 5 psi, representing an approximate 39% reduction in error compared to the baseline linear regression. Explainable AI analysis revealed that phase angle was the most significant parameter in predicting DM, followed by aggregate gradation and binder characteristics. Overall, the findings show that the DM of HMA is influenced by complex nonlinear interactions among multiple factors. The AI-based models provided higher predictive accuracy and insights into interactions among material properties, supporting the development of optimized asphalt mix design guidelines for durable pavements.

Predictive process monitoring (PPM) typically forecasts the future of individual process instances, hence operating on trace level. Process managers, however, typically operate on process level, e.g., when assigning staff or calculating KPIs. The question is how well such process-level managerial decisions are supported by existing approaches, given that PPM research has so far not focused on process-level predictions. We answer this question through a comprehensive benchmarking study of two process-level prediction tasks: concurrent trace prediction and average throughput time prediction. Across synthetic and real-life event logs, we compare statistical and machine-learning-based methods, foundation models, business process simulation, and, importantly, established trace-level PPM approaches, aggregating their predictions to the process-level. We assess which modeling paradigms are most suitable for predicting process-level behavior and whether existing trace-level PPM can be effectively repurposed for this task. Our results show substantial variation in performance across approaches. Notably, aggregated trace-level predictions cause errors to compound on process-level, reducing accuracy and highlighting process-level prediction as a distinct predictive task that warrants dedicated research.

Background Mosquito-borne diseases remain a major global public health challenge, with expanding geographic distribution driven by climate change, urbanization, and environmental modifications. Accurate forecasting of mosquito vector populations is essential for effective surveillance and control. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) approaches have emerged as promising tools for modelling complex, nonlinear relationships in vector ecology. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the predictive performance of AI and ML models applied to mosquito vector surveillance worldwide and to summarize comparative evidence with traditional statistical methods where directly reported. Methods Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, and Scopus was conducted up to August 2025. Studies modelling mosquito vectors (Aedes, Culex, Anopheles) using AI/ML techniques were included. Data on study characteristics, modelling approaches, predictors, and performance metrics (e.g., AUC, sensitivity, specificity, RMSE, R 2 ) were extracted. Results were primarily synthesized descriptively because of substantial methodological and clinical/ecological heterogeneity. Exploratory random-effects meta-analyses were conducted for commonly reported performance metrics, with pooled estimates interpreted alongside measures of between-study heterogeneity and prediction intervals. Risk of bias was assessed using a PROBAST-informed assessment adapted to the ecological and entomological context. Results Seventy-one studies were included, spanning diverse geographic regions and ecological settings. Random Forest was the most frequently used algorithm. Reported predictive performance varied substantially across studies and prediction tasks, with AUC values ranging from 0.61 to 0.99. Exploratory quantitative syntheses showed exceptionally high between-study heterogeneity, limiting the generalizability of pooled performance estimates. Most studies relied on internal validation, with limited use of external validation, further limiting assessment of model performance across independent surveillance settings. Conclusions AI and ML approaches show potential for supporting mosquito vector surveillance, but reported predictive performance varies substantially across prediction tasks, taxa, ecological settings, and validation frameworks. The extreme heterogeneity observed across studies limits the generalizability of pooled performance estimates and precludes broad conclusions regarding the predictive performance of AI/ML approaches across surveillance settings. Methodological standardization, transparent reporting, external validation across independent settings, and direct comparisons with conventional statistical approaches are needed to establish the reliability and real-world applicability of these models. documents.abstract: Personalized vision-language assistants use visual observations and personal memories to provide advice tailored to the user. When the observed scene contains a physical hazard, personal context, such as allergies, medical conditions, or mobility constraints, can change what help is appropriate. Responding appropriately therefore requires recognizing the visible hazard and applying the relevant person's information. We introduce PReMind-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that evaluates this combination across diverse hazards and personal-memory conditions. It separately measures memory access, grounding, abstention, and hazard response, and assesses joint success on interdependency cases. Existing models often satisfy one requirement while failing the other, and training only for safety or personalization leaves a gap in joint success. We therefore propose PReMind, a two-phase reinforcement learning framework that combines on-demand and forced-call interactions (memory always retrieved) to jointly train grounded memory use and hazard response. At 4B, PReMind raises joint success from 12.9% to 28.6% over its base on the interdependency set and improves hazard adequacy and correct abstention on the main test. Joint-success gains persist under forced-call evaluation and under a second LLM judge across three Phase II seeds; averaged over these seeds, joint success also improves on unseen hazard groups. These findings highlight the need to evaluate and train personal assistants to connect visual evidence with the relevant person's context.

This conceptual paper introduces Preservation of Reopening Conditions Through Provisional Closure, an account of how inquiry can end for the purposes of action while retaining a planned route for later reopening. The mechanism consists in preserving an unresolved dependency, a condition that would warrant reconsideration, and an accessible route through which relevant evidence can be detected, connected to the closed question, and brought to someone able to act. The paper assesses provisional closure by whether the specified trigger can be detected, linked to the prior issue, and translated into a feasible step of reopening. It distinguishes retaining these conditions from their subsequent use: storage alone does not ensure monitoring, recognition, authority, or action. It also separates preserving a route back from the later conversion of detected discrepancy into effective revision. The account concerns consequential unresolved dependencies and does not require every conclusion to remain provisional. The mechanism is situated alongside Charles S. Peirce’s account of inquiry as the settlement of doubt and examined through two documented cases. Olympic anti-doping sample storage preserves material for later reanalysis when new information or improved detection methods become available. Japan’s conditional, time-limited approval of HeartSheet required follow-up and reapplication with survival evidence; the submitted analysis did not demonstrate superiority on its primary endpoint, and regular approval was refused. These cases are interpreted through published studies and institutional reports, with attention to the retained evidence, review conditions, and authority required to reopen a settled decision. Part of the Recursive Inquiry and Encounter series within On Human Modeling, the paper examines who retains and monitors reopening conditions, who can authorize reconsideration, and who bears the continuing cost of maintaining a route back. Potential applications in human–AI research include preserving assumption records, specifying review triggers, routing later evidence to responsible decision makers, and designing processes through which decisions can return to active inquiry.

Tabular in-context learning (TabICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to predict target records using a handful of labeled demonstrations in their prompts. However, these demonstrations often contain sensitive personal information. Differential privacy (DP) offers principled protection, but noise-based methods introduce substantial noise, distorting the feature-label relationships essential for accurate prediction, especially as data dimensionality grows. In this work, we study DP data synthesis for generating privacy-preserving TabICL demonstrations. We identify two limitations of directly applying general-purpose DP synthesis to entire datasets: modeling a global distribution can obscure local structure and minority patterns in heterogeneous data, while measuring broad attribute dependencies under a limited privacy budget can reduce the accuracy available for relationships most relevant to prediction. More broadly, global statistical fidelity may fail to preserve heterogeneous structures needed by downstream predictive and generative models. To address these challenges, we propose PriTabICL, a general framework compatible with existing DP synthesis algorithms. It partitions records into DP clusters and synthesizes each independently, using a fixed feature-target workload to prioritize prediction-relevant statistical relationships. At inference, each query is routed to a DP cluster, and demonstrations are sampled from its synthetic dataset without additional privacy loss for the original records. Experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods across heterogeneous datasets. In particular, one of our instantiations, PriTabICL-PrivSyn, improves over global PrivSyn in 8 out of 12 settings and outperforms existing private TabICL approaches in nearly all evaluated settings. Open-source code is available.

Patient history taking is a strategic, multi-turn process that refines diagnostic hypotheses through iterative questioning, mirroring clinical reasoning where each inquiry updates beliefs over candidate diagnoses. Deploying AI in this setting is constrained by privacy, cost, and latency, making Small Language Models (SLMs) a more desirable backbone compared to larger LLMs. However, SLMs capture only the fast, intuitive "System 1" side of this process and lack explicit mechanisms for the deliberative "System 2" reasoning needed to maintain and update diagnostic uncertainty over time. Bayesian Networks (BayesNets) offer a natural complement, providing an interpretable framework for auditable probabilistic belief tracking. Yet, clinical BayesNets are difficult to construct due to their reliance on expert curated structure, dependencies, and parameters. We introduce ProbMedTOD, which automatically synthesizes a clinical BayesNet from a small number of clinical notes in three stages: ontology building, structure prediction, and parameter estimation. ProbMedTOD then integrates the resulting BayesNet with SLMs, enabling probabilistic reasoning in multi-turn dialogues. A BayesNet Agent maintains real-time posterior distributions over diagnoses, while a Policy Agent picks diagnostically informative questions. Experiments on DDXPlus and MIMIC-IV Notes show that ProbMedTOD outperforms LLM-only and retrieval-based baselines, with especially strong gains for smaller models.
