documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can expand the range of candidate solutions available during design exploration, but it can also obscure whether students have engaged in the iterative design reasoning and evaluative judgement that studio teaching is intended to develop. This article examines how GenAI can be integrated into creative media education without displacing the cognitive processes through which creative expertise is cultivated. It draws on design research, automation literature, and cognitive load theory, alongside illustrative teaching cases spanning undergraduate and postgraduate animation, visual effects, and game design curricula at Auckland University of Technology and The Hong Kong Polytechnic University. We argue that the educational value of GenAI depends not on the sophistication of its outputs alone, but on whether students retain responsibility for evaluative judgement throughout the design process. We propose Process Before Prompting, a pedagogical framework intended to preserve this responsibility within human-led cycles of divergence, convergence, and appreciative judgement. Students establish an initial creative intention before engaging with GenAI and remain responsible for interpreting, refining, and selecting among both human- and AI-generated candidates. This framework offers practical guidance for scaffolding independent judgement and assessing evidence of iterative design reasoning within existing studio teaching practices.

Introduction Attribution theory explains how audiences use observable information to infer otherwise unobservable agents and processes behind creative work. This study applied this perspective to examine how production-source disclosures influence source-role perceptions, higher-order creative attributions, and audience reception of two-dimensional animation. Methods In a randomized experiment, 626 adults were assigned to one of four production-source disclosure conditions—undisclosed, human-made, human–AI collaborative, or AI-led—while viewing the same three animation clips, all of which were actually produced through human–AI collaboration. We examined between-condition differences in source-role perceptions, higher-order creative attributions, and audience-reception outcomes, as well as concurrent associations between higher-order creative attributions and audience reception. Results The disclosures clearly differentiated participants’ perceptions of AI and human involvement. Perceived creative effort was statistically significant before correction but did not meet the α = 0.05 criterion after Holm adjustment ( p = 0.0502); the only corrected contrast indicated lower perceived creative effort in the human–AI collaborative condition than in the human-made condition. No statistically reliable omnibus between-condition differences emerged for perceived authorship, perceived emotional authenticity, artistic evaluation, situational immersion, or viewing and recommendation intention. Higher-order creative attributions were positively associated with all three audience-reception indicators in concurrent analyses, although the strong correlation between perceived emotional authenticity and situational immersion warrants caution about measurement overlap. Discussion The findings indicate that the diagnosticity of a production-source cue depends on the judgment target: the disclosures clearly reorganized perceived production roles but did not yield statistically reliable corresponding differences across most higher-order creative attributions or reception outcomes. The attribution–reception relations represent concurrent covariation rather than causal mediation. Because the three clips were presented in a fixed order, material and order effects cannot be separated, and the equivalence analyses did not establish negligible between-condition differences.

The World Health Organization (WHO) identifies high blood pressure (hypertension) as a major global public health concern and a significant risk factor for cardiovascular diseases. Therefore, facial Shiatsu massage can be a good solution to alleviate them. However, most people are not only unfamiliar with the locations of acupressure points for proper massage but also lack motivation to conduct it regularly. In this paper, we propose a facial Shiatsu massage exergame system as an effective approach to solve these conditions together. The system runs on a low-cost PC with a camera, provides a simple quiz on a selective topic, and recognizes an answer gesture of a player to select one choice to each question. A generative AI-based quiz generator is implemented to automatically generate quiz questions across different categories providing flexible and varied educational content for the proposed smart healthcare exergame system. An answer gesture is defined for pressing a proper acupressure point with an index finger, which is recognized by applying a MediaPipe library to a user’s face image taken by a PC camera. In this paper, four gestures are implemented to select one of the four choices in each question. For accuracy evaluation, first, we implemented the answer gesture recognition program and investigated the gesture recognition accuracy. Then, for effectiveness evaluation, we implemented the quiz generator using Ollama, produced quizzes on Japanese History, Simple Arithmetic, Indonesian Words, and Taiwan Geography with 50 questions for each topic, and asked 20 persons to use the system. For each user, we measured health condition-related indices such as blood pressure, body temperature, and facial skin moisture level before and after the system use by each person. In addition, we conducted a questionnaire and calculated the Usability and User Experience score. These results indicate the potential feasibility of the proposed system.

Background: Prosthesis users report high cognitive workload, or the mental effort needed to achieve task performance. The NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) is the most common subjective workload measure. However, it was developed for general human–machine interfaces and may not capture prosthesis-specific demands. The recently proposed Prosthesis Task Load Index (PROS-TLX) includes additional domains relevant to prosthesis use, yet its psychometric properties have not been established. This study compared the convergent validity, test-retest reliability, and measurement error of the NASA-TLX and PROS-TLX across two groups.Methods: Ten individuals without limb difference performed a timed reach-and-grasp task using a myoelectric prosthetic emulator in both a physical and virtual environment. Additionally, ten individuals with upper limb difference performed an accuracy- and time-based activity of daily living using their customary myoelectric, multi-grip prosthesis. Both groups completed two sessions at least a week apart and rated workload using the NASA-TLX and the PROS-TLX in both sessions. Because the PROS-TLX has more total subscales, we modified the scoring of the PROS-TLX to align it with the NASA-TLX. For both surveys, total workload scores were a weighted average of the subscales, ranging from low (0) to high (100). We compared total workload scores between the surveys using Pearson's correlation and calculated the intraclass correlation coefficients, measurement error, and minimum detectable change for each survey. We also explored the role of session number, survey, and task environment on the survey subscales and the relationships between subscales and task performance outcomes.Results: For emulator users, the PROS-TLX and NASA-TLX total workload scores were moderately correlated in session 1 (r>0.63), suggesting good convergent validity. However, for prosthesis users, the surveys were weakly correlated in session 1 (r=0.13). The PROS-TLX demonstrated higher test–retest reliability point estimates (ICC=0.44–0.83) and lower measurement error (SEM=7.43-10.79) than NASA-TLX (ICC=0.18-0.45, SEM=10.52-17.29), though the confidence intervals were large. The prosthesis-specific subscale of uncertainty varied by task environment and correlated with performance outcomes.Conclusions: The PROS-TLX adds prosthesis-specific contributors to workload to the NASA-TLX with higher reliability and lower measurement error estimates, but wide confidence intervals limit conclusions. Larger studies in prosthesis users are needed.

Accurate marine target detection is essential for maritime situational awareness and safe navigation by unmanned surface vehicles. However, uneven radar returns and uncertain spatial correspondence complicate radar–camera fusion, while input-level integration does not explicitly adapt subsequent feature processing to local radar evidence. We propose QPAFusion, which refines multi-scale features through query-guided local radar sampling and adaptively aggregates feature branches using radar priors. On the WaterScenes dataset, QPAFusion achieves 64.5%mAP50−−95 and 90.9%mAP50, exceeding the reported three-frame REVP fusion baseline by 2.0 and 2.1 percentage points, respectively, with mAP50 gains of 6.4 and 3.1 percentage points on the adverse-lighting and adverse-weather subsets. These results support combining local-radar refinement with adaptive feature aggregation for object detection on the water surface, with larger accuracy gains on the evaluated adverse-condition subsets.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly becoming embedded in higher education systems, influencing teaching, assessment, research, and institutional decision-making. Despite the growing adoption of AI, existing governance approaches remain largely principle-based, emphasizing ethical guidelines such as transparency, accountability, and fairness without providing operational mechanisms for implementation within quality assurance (QA) and accreditation systems. This creates a critical gap between AI governance principles and the procedural structures through which educational quality and institutional accountability are evaluated. This study addresses this gap by developing an operational quality assurance framework to systematically integrate AI governance into a ten-step higher education accreditation lifecycle, with explicitly differentiated AI permission levels and defined boundaries for human evaluative authority. Using a conceptual and policy-synthesis approach, the study integrates global AI governance principles, established QA standards, and accreditation practices into a risk-based, human-centered governance model. The framework operationalizes AI governance and integration through a model that defines the role, boundaries, and permissible levels of AI use across each stage of the accreditation process. A central feature of the model is the explicit preservation of human decision-making authority in evaluative and high-stakes accreditation stages. The study reconceptualizes AI integration in higher education as a quality assurance and governance challenge rather than solely a technological innovation problem. By embedding AI governance and integrating it directly within accreditation processes, the proposed model provides a practical bridge between ethical principles and operational implementation. The proposed framework provides a structured basis for quality assurance agencies, regulators, and higher education institutions to consider risk-based AI governance within accreditation processes, with its feasibility, effectiveness, and transferability requiring further evaluation through implementation and empirical validation.

Abstract Many tabular classification tasks involve imbalanced classes, but synthetic oversampling can produce rows that violate feature constraints or duplicate existing observations. We present QualSynth, a training-free framework that prompts a large language model to make sparse edits to real minority-class rows under data-derived feature constraints and a machine-readable output contract. A deterministic validation layer checks each candidate’s structure, values, and duplication before admitting it to the training set. We evaluated QualSynth on eight benchmark datasets with ten seeds against four synthetic oversamplers, including the widely used SMOTE, and class-weighted learning without augmentation. QualSynth achieved the highest F1 score among the synthetic oversamplers on four datasets, while SMOTE had the best average ranks. In equivalence tests, QualSynth and SMOTE differed by less than prespecified margins of 0.03 in F1 score and 0.02 in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC). After correction for multiple comparisons, the only pairwise difference was higher ROC-AUC for QualSynth than for the diffusion model TabDDPM. Class weighting alone had the best overall ranks, and no augmentation strategy improved aggregate ROC-AUC over the unweighted reference. QualSynth is therefore a controlled, inspectable option for minority-class augmentation, with predictive utility comparable to SMOTE’s.

Raman spectroscopy is one of the most accessible vibrational probes in materials laboratories, but its forward problem (structure to spectrum) is bottlenecked by the cost of density functional perturbation theory, and its inverse problem (spectrum to structure) typically relies on retrieval against curated references. We introduce RamanGPT, a deep-learning framework that addresses both directions for crystalline inorganic materials. The forward model, an Atomistic Line Graph Neural Network (ALIGNN), is trained on the 5,099-material Computational Raman Database and predicts 200-bin spectra over 50–1000 $$\hbox {cm}^{-1}$$ with 53.8% of the 509 held-out materials reaching an active-region cosine similarity of at least 0.354, capturing qualitative features of the target spectrum. The model also shows qualitative agreement with an experimental measurement of metallic 1T $$\hbox {VSe}_{2}$$ , a system absent from the training set. The inverse model fine-tunes DiffractGPT, a large language model already trained for diffraction-to-structure generation, via Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation on Raman-plus-formula prompts, recovering lattice parameters with mean absolute errors of 1.13–2.14 Å and reduced-formula consistency of 92.1% on 508 held-out materials, compared to 17.1% for a formula-conditioned retrieval baseline given identical inputs. A cosine-similarity matcher and an inverse $$\rightarrow$$ relax $$\rightarrow$$ forward consistency loop are deployed at https://atomgpt.org/raman .

documents.abstract: The digital-intelligent transformation of traditional calligraphy education is advancing through the integration of artificial intelligence, big data, and immersive technologies. This study proposes a Dual Helix Reconstruction Model that synergistically couples a data chain with a teaching chain, establishing a closed-loop learning ecosystem incorporating intelligent handwriting analysis, contextual immersion, and collaborative feedback. A longitudinal experiment conducted in an authentic calligraphy course demonstrated the model's efficacy through multisource evidence. Results showed significant improvements in writing precision (d = 0.91), fluency (d = 0.85), and learning motivation (d = 0.88), confirming its role in enhancing skill acquisition, engagement, and self-regulation. Furthermore, the model fostered the integrated development of artistic expression and cultural understanding. This research provides a replicable paradigm for the digital-intelligent evolution of calligraphy education and contributes a methodological foundation for interdisciplinary innovation in art pedagogy.

Mountainous linear cultural heritage corridors include both formal-access and restricted-access sections, but recreation perceptions across these settings remain insufficiently understood. Using 17,034 online reviews from 18 Ming Great Wall sections in the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region, China, this study compared perception-element prominence, sentiment orientations, and textual co-occurrence through an integrated analytical framework, LLM-assisted labelling, statistical comparisons, section-level sensitivity analyses, and co-occurrence networks. Embodied recreation was prominent in both settings. Section-level comparisons showed greater attention to management and services, particularly entry costs and infrastructure, in formal-access sections, whereas mountain environments and risk and use impacts were more prominent in restricted-access sections, particularly naturalness and heritage preservation. Although sentiment profiles differed descriptively, no section-level sentiment comparisons remained significant after multiple-testing correction. Co-occurrence analysis revealed associations between infrastructure and embodied recreation in formal-access reviews, while restricted-access reviews linked heritage preservation, mountain environments, bodily activity, and safety concerns. By extending recreation-perception analysis beyond formally managed attractions, this study provides comparative evidence of shared recreational interests and differentiated management concerns within a continuous heritage corridor. The findings inform access-sensitive management and corridor-scale heritage conservation, subject to limitations associated with platform coverage and reviewer self-selection.

There is an ontological shift currently taking place in the modern workplace due to AI and collaborative technologies. The classical theories of human relations, which rely on human interaction and human co-presence, fail to explain the relational issues involved in the modern hybrid human-AI workplace environment. This paper proposes a theoretical framework known as the Post-Human Relations Theoretical Framework (PHRTF). The PHRTF is conceptualised using post-humanist organisational theory, actor-network theory, sociotechnical systems analysis, and sociology of work and technology. In light of the systematic theoretical synthesis and review of empirical papers written between 2015 and 2024, the study finds four interrelated foundations of the post-human relational ecosystem: distributed agency and relational ontology; affective infrastructure and hybrid trust; temporal-spatial dislocation and presence reconstitution; and algorithmic authority and moral accountability. The framework challenges classical human relations’ anthropocentrism, arguing that ethical, productive AI-workplace relationships require a new understanding of relational actors.

Public benchmarks support comparisons of large language model (LLM) capabilities, yet users can experience the same highly ranked model differently. Drawing on traditional software reliability, we argue that the reliability of an LLM service should be assessed for specified users and conditions of use. This requires more than a capability score: evaluation evidence must support a claim about failure during future operation. We distinguish testing to discover faults from testing to assess reliability and identify ten modelling considerations behind such claims. We propose a six-workstream research roadmap linking claim specification, dynamic operational profiles, graded outcomes and noisy judgements, local probabilistic robustness, interaction dependence, and statistical inference with reassessment. Local probabilistic robustness addresses the behavioural variation hidden when different concrete inputs are treated as the same task. Published findings and an illustrative customer-support example motivate the roadmap; its integrated validation remains an open research task. Reliability claims complement, but do not replace, separate safety and security arguments. Capability scores should therefore be complemented by versioned operational claims that state whose requirements are covered, under which conditions, and with what uncertainty.

Gamification has become increasingly prominent in technology-mediated language education, yet the field’s development, knowledge base, and current thematic directions remain insufficiently mapped. This study examines publication growth, major contributors, intellectual foundations, current research …

Today, many educational institutions are incorporating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into their curricula, although skepticism is increasing among younger generations, particularly in Australia and the United States. Some students are organizing opposition to the use of generative AI in coursework. The creative industry continues to experiment with AI-based production methods, and art museums and film festivals are featuring AI-generated works. Countries such as China maintain a highly optimistic perspective on the technology. This panel convenes experts from Australia, China, South Korea, and the United States to examine critical questions regarding the role of AI in education and the arts.

Background: High-potential incidents in construction are often initially understood through the actions of the person closest to the event. This can narrow investigations, obscure the operational and organisational conditions that shaped performance, and weaken both learning and trust. As HEB Construction’s Critical Control Management programme matured, the organisation identified a disconnect between its prevention approach and the way incidents, individual actions and accountability were considered. Aim: This practice case study describes the development and implementation of Responding Fairly, an approach intended to connect Critical Control Management, Incident Cause Analysis Method investigations, Human and Organisational Performance principles, and people processes. Its purpose is to support fair, consistent and evidence-informed decisions while maintaining accountability. Approach: Rather than introducing a separate process, HEB aligned existing investigation, critical control and people practices around a shared sequence of questions. Investigations first consider which controls should have prevented the event, whether those controls were present and effective, how the work was designed and supported, and which conditions influenced decisions at the time. Individual actions are considered after this context has been established. The approach is jointly supported by Operations, Health and Safety, and Human Resources, with leader coaching and practical guidance used to strengthen consistency. Practice example and findings: A service-strike investigation showed how an apparent failure by an operator was better understood when outdated plans, a changed work scope, conflicting site markings, unavailable technical support and time pressure were examined together. This broader analysis led to strengthened service verification requirements, revalidation following scope changes and clearer excavation controls. Early implementation experience indicates richer learning, more targeted corrective actions, greater leader confidence and improved worker perceptions of fairness. Conclusion: Responding Fairly demonstrates how prevention, investigation and accountability can be treated as one connected learning system. Context does not remove accountability; it enables accountability to be located more fairly and supported by fuller evidence. The experience also suggests that a framework alone is insufficient: leaders require capability, support and confidence to pause, tolerate uncertainty and understand the conditions surrounding an event before reaching conclusions.

The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into organizational practices has raised important questions about responsible leadership, knowledge integration, and employee innovation. This study examined the relationship between responsible AI leadership and employee idea implementation …

This conceptual paper introduces Responsive Cues Converted Into Reciprocal Obligation, a mechanism through which repeated signs of attention can lead someone to feel that care is owed in either direction. A device that comes when called or asks to be held may come to seem like a companion who depends on its owner. The owner, in turn, may expect someone to keep that companion functioning. The mechanism concerns the point at which such an expectation extends beyond any commitment established by the people or institutions behind the device. The paper places this account alongside Byron Reeves and Clifford Nass’s work on how people apply social conventions to computers and other media. It asks what a particular person came to expect, which words or actions connect that expectation to a responsive cue, and who undertook to honor it. A person’s account of companionship can establish what the relationship meant to them. A provider’s statements and policies supply evidence about what that provider promised. Sony’s AIBO illustrates the distinction. Sony offered repairs for its earlier models for stated periods, and its repair clinic operated beyond the latest deadline in its notice. In 2018, owners of the new aibo asked Sony to extend its policy of providing repairs for seven years after withdrawal from sale. The founder of A FUN, an independent repair firm, argued that Sony bore continuing responsibility for the companion it had brought to market. The paper leaves the merits of that demand open. GROOVE X’s LOVOT provides a contrast through priced care plans whose written terms specify what the maker will cover. Part of the Presence Through Technology series within On Human Modeling, the paper also offers a way to examine expectations of discretion in human–AI interaction. A conversational assistant might recall a private concern and ask about it weeks later. If the user explains that being remembered led them to expect the exchange to stay private, that account connects a specific cue to a specific expectation. The provider’s confidentiality commitments can then be compared with what the user understood.

The correspondence of Heinrich Bullinger (1504-1575), Swiss Reformer and Antistes of Zurich, documents the political and religious debates of the Reformation, including extensive appeals to the Church Fathers as authoritative sources. Detecting such references computationally remains largely unexplored. We investigate dense and sparse retrieval for patristic reference detection, and metadata-informed topic modelling as a proxy for the topics and ideas discussed. Prior work on Latin intertextuality has fine-tuned dense retrievers for their respective target domain, and we test how well these models transfer to Bullinger's correspondence. We compare lexical (BM25), dense (bi-encoders), and hybrid methods on explicit and implicit references. A Latin encoder fine-tuned on biblical reuse performs best among the bi-encoders (82%, Recall@20 on explicit and 16% on implicit references), while BM25 outperforms dense approaches on explicit citations (94%, R@20). Because BM25 and dense retrieval recover disjoint sets of implicit references, fusing their rankings raises implicit R@20 to 22%, close to cross-encoder reranking of the same candidates (26%) but without its inference cost. For topic modelling, we extend FASTopic with a seed-guided loss function and editorial abstract embeddings. Measurable coherence gains over the baseline remain minimal, but qualitative and temporal analysis shows that some topics track documented historical events. However, dominant topic weights barely exceed a uniform distribution, making topics unusable to inform retrieval. A pilot application of LLM-based concept induction (LLooM) further points towards a more human-interpretable alternative. Together, these results present a first approach to retrieving patristic references and modelling fine-grained topics in Bullinger's correspondence.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often store document chunks in a vector index together with a copy of their access-control metadata. When a user's permission is revoked in the authoritative permission store, this indexed copy may remain stale, allowing the vector database to keep returning protected content. This paper measures the duration of this revocation window and separates two outcomes: unauthorized index retrieval, in which the vector database returns a protected chunk, and LLM-context exposure, in which that chunk reaches the context assembled for the language model. We built a controlled synthetic testbed with PostgreSQL as the authoritative permission store and Qdrant as the vector index, and evaluated six enforcement configurations: periodic synchronization, event-driven synchronization, a no-worker control, query-time authorization, hybrid authorization, and query-time authorization with a 10-second decision cache. Each configuration retained 27 trials (5 for the control) within a 35-second observation window. The median context-level revocation propagation time was 9.92 s for 20-second periodic synchronization, 14 ms for event-driven synchronization, and 4.98 s for the cached query-time configuration. Under periodic synchronization, 87.7% of relevant queries placed the protected chunk in the context before revocation was enforced. Query-time and hybrid authorization blocked protected content at the first post-revocation probe (0 ms at probe resolution) even though the stale index kept returning it, while the no-worker control never achieved stable enforcement within the window. These findings describe the tested synthetic testbed and are not production guarantees.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a technology with tremendous potential to revolutionize healthcare, contributing to progress in medical diagnostics, clinical decision support, personalized medicine, patient monitoring, medical research, and healthcare management. This systematic review covers the current use of AI in healthcare, its clinical effects and hindrances for implementation. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines were followed to conduct a systematic literature search. The search query was conducted in major electronic databases using specific keywords of the studies and results, such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and other sources, including studies on artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, large language models, healthcare applications, clinical decision support, medical imaging, drug discovery, digital health, and healthcare data systems. This evidence review identifies evidence of how AI is being used in a variety of healthcare areas such as medical imaging and diagnostics, virtual patient monitoring, drug design, precision medicine, rehabilitation, patient engagement, and operational health care processes. The use of AI has been shown to have the potential to enhance the accuracy of diagnosis, improve clinical decision‐making, personalize care, and optimize healthcare workflows. However, there are substantial hurdles to overcome, such as data privacy and security issues, algorithmic bias, the lack of the clinical validation of AI models, regulatory scrutiny, infrastructure challenges, and the need for effective clinical validation. The key takeaways from this review are the need for a balanced approach to the integration of AI in healthcare, acknowledging both the technological innovations and the ethical, regulatory, and human factors considerations that need to be addressed. More large‐scale clinical validation studies are needed as well as the establishment of reliable AI systems and strategies to ensure responsible and fair use of AI in healthcare.
